days.title: Bundle Project Structure, Shared Python Code and Dependency Failures

concepts.heading: One Entry File, Many Files, and What Gets Synced
concepts.body: A bundle has exactly one entry file, `databricks.yml`. At professional depth the trap is mixing up three similarly named mappings. The top-level `include` lists additional bundle configuration files, such as `resources/*.yml`; a file that no glob matches is never parsed, so validation passes and its job or pipeline silently never deploys. `sync.include` and `sync.exclude` filter which files are uploaded, and `sync.paths` adds folders that sit outside the bundle root. Deployment uploads the files under the root, so a shared package in `libs/common_transforms/` beside the bundle folder never reaches the workspace unless the folder is added to `sync.paths` (the bundle root is still synced). Symptom: `ModuleNotFoundError` after a successful deploy. A large estate also needs repetition. A For each task repeats work at run time inside one job, with one schedule and one set of alerts. Python support for bundles creates one real job resource per table at deploy time from a metadata file, each with its own schedule, owner permissions and alerts.

concepts.heading: Building Wheels and Keeping Versions Fresh
concepts.body: Bundles can build a Python wheel through an `artifacts` mapping with `type: whl` and a build command, then attach it to job tasks. On serverless compute the environment of a task is cached, and Python identifies a wheel by name and version. A rebuilt wheel that still says `0.1.0` looks identical to the installed one, so the job keeps running old code. The serverless documentation states that changing a custom package requires updating its version number. For the bundle workflow, setting `dynamic_version: true` on the wheel artifact patches the version from the timestamp of the built file, so CI can redeploy without anyone editing `pyproject.toml`. Where the wheel is stored matters too. The DBFS root is writable by any workspace user, so storing libraries there is deprecated and disabled by default on current runtimes. Workspace files, Unity Catalog volumes or a package repository are the recommended homes. A volume is governed by privileges, so only a release service principal needs write access while jobs only read.

concepts.heading: Pipelines Resolve Dependencies Differently from Jobs
concepts.body: A job task can install the project through an environment or a libraries entry. A Lakeflow Pipelines pipeline does not behave the same way: its dependencies are declared in the pipeline's `environment` section, for example a pinned package or a wheel path in a Unity Catalog volume. Adding a library only to `pyproject.toml` leaves a pipeline failing with `ModuleNotFoundError` after redeploy. Pipelines support only SQL and Python. JVM libraries are not supported in pipelines, and installing them, even through an init script, causes unpredictable behavior, so run the JVM step as its own task on suitable compute that writes a Unity Catalog table, and let a later pipeline task read it. Serverless pipelines do not support init scripts at all. Even on classic compute, Databricks recommends the Environment settings, because external dependencies and init scripts raise the risk of breakage when the runtime upgrades. Pin versions, install wheels from a `/Volumes/...` path, and test the pipeline automatically.

concepts.heading: Why Serverless Installs Fail
concepts.body: Serverless installs fail for a few repeatable reasons. First, Spark is part of the managed environment: installing PySpark, or any package that depends on it, stops the session before code runs. Package authors should list PySpark as a development dependency instead of a hard runtime requirement. Second, serverless does not pin a CPU architecture. A task can land on `aarch64` or `x86_64`, and the choice can change between runs. A wheel with native extensions is built for one architecture, so installs fail intermittently with unchanged code. Prefer pure-Python wheels, or ship both variants each constrained with a `platform_machine` marker. Third, dependencies are resolved before notebook code runs, and serverless has no compute-scoped environment variables, so setting `PIP_INDEX_URL` in a cell changes nothing. For a private mirror put `index-url` or `extra-index-url` in the dependency specification, or ask an admin to configure default package repositories. Diagnose by asking whether the failure happens before any user code runs.

examPoints: A question about modules missing after a successful deploy is testing `sync.paths` for folders outside the bundle root, or `include` for configuration files that were never parsed.

A job that keeps running old code from a rebuilt wheel is testing the unchanged version number and `dynamic_version`; a pipeline that cannot find a library is testing the pipeline `environment` section.

Intermittent install errors with native wheels point to architecture variants, a session that dies at setup points to PySpark in the dependency tree, and a private mirror needs `index-url` in the specification, not an environment variable in a cell.

quiz.q: A bundle's job imports a package from `libs/common_transforms/`, a sibling of the bundle folder. After `bundle deploy` the job fails with `ModuleNotFoundError`. Which change fixes it?
choices: Add the folder to the top-level `include` mapping so the CLI reads its configuration
Add `../libs` to `sync.paths` so the folder is uploaded
Add the folder to `sync.exclude` so the CLI stops filtering the files from the upload
Copy the package into the DBFS root and set a cluster environment variable that points at it for every task
quiz.explain: `sync.paths` lets the sync include folders outside the bundle root. The top-level `include` only references bundle configuration files, `sync.exclude` removes files from the upload, and the DBFS root is a deprecated, overwritable library location.

quiz.q: A team rebuilds an internal wheel and redeploys; the serverless job keeps running the old behavior because the version in `pyproject.toml` never changes. What is the best fix?
choices: Set `dynamic_version: true` on the wheel artifact to patch its version
Switch the job to a classic cluster policy, because serverless never installs wheels from volumes
Set `PIP_INDEX_URL` in the first notebook cell so the task fetches the newest wheel at start
Install PySpark into the task environment so the wheel is rebuilt whenever the job session starts up
quiz.explain: The cached serverless environment treats the same name and version as already installed, so a new timestamped version forces a fresh install. The other options misdescribe volumes, run too late to affect dependency resolution, or break the session.

days.recap: Know which bundle mapping does what (`include` for configuration, `sync.paths` for code), keep wheel versions moving, declare pipeline libraries in `environment`, and read serverless install errors as PySpark, architecture or index problems.

days.title: UDFs: Pandas, Python, SQL and Unity Catalog Functions

concepts.heading: Choosing Between Built-ins and UDFs
concepts.body: Built-in Spark functions run inside the engine and are optimized for distributed processing. A Python UDF moves data between the JVM and a Python process, which is expensive at scale. The documentation recommends UDFs for ad hoc queries, manual data cleaning, exploratory work and small to medium datasets, and recommends built-in methods for large datasets and for anything that runs regularly or continuously, such as ETL and streaming. The professional decision therefore starts with a question: can a built-in express this? A regular expression extraction on three billion rows every hour belongs to `regexp_extract`, not to a Python UDF whose time shows up as serialization in the Spark UI. Use a UDF when logic is hard to express with built-ins, for example encryption, hashing, JSON parsing or validation. When a UDF is justified, pick the vectorized form: pandas UDFs transfer data with Apache Arrow and work on batches, which the documentation describes as vastly faster than row-by-row Python UDFs.

concepts.heading: Pandas UDF Flavors and Expensive Initialization
concepts.body: A pandas UDF receives pandas objects per Arrow batch. A Series to Series UDF is called once per batch, so anything initialized in its body repeats for every batch. When a function needs a large object such as a 600 MB model loaded from a volume, executors can spend most of their time deserializing it. The Iterator of Series to Iterator of Series variant takes an iterator of batches and yields output batches, so the model can be loaded once before the loop and reused for every batch in that task. The length of the whole output must equal the length of the whole input. Wrap the loop in `try/finally` when a resource has to be released. Related forms such as `mapInPandas`, `mapInArrow` and `applyInPandas` apply a function to whole DataFrames or groups rather than to a single column. The exam question is usually the symptom: repeated loading cost means move the initialization out of the per-batch call.

concepts.heading: Unity Catalog Functions: Privileges, Compute and Isolation
concepts.body: A Unity Catalog function is a governed object named `catalog.schema.function`, written in SQL or Python. Creating one needs `USAGE` and `CREATE` on the schema plus `USAGE` on the catalog. Running one needs `EXECUTE` on the function plus `USAGE` on the schema and catalog. Python code in these UDFs needs a serverless or pro SQL warehouse, or a cluster on a supported runtime; a view that includes a Unity Catalog Python UDF fails on a classic SQL warehouse even when every privilege is granted. So when a UDF works in a notebook and fails in a dashboard, compare the compute type before touching grants. By default, Python UDFs with the same owner and session can share an isolation environment, which saves memory. The `STRICT ISOLATION` characteristic guarantees that a UDF runs in its own isolated environment; add it to UDFs that run input as code with `exec()` or `eval()`, write local files, change global state or access environment variables.

concepts.heading: Evaluation Order and Null Handling
concepts.body: Spark SQL, including the DataFrame API, does not guarantee the order in which subexpressions are evaluated. Inputs of an operator are not necessarily evaluated left to right, and `AND` and `OR` have no guaranteed short-circuiting. The optimizer can reorder predicates in `WHERE` and `HAVING`, so a UDF may receive rows that an earlier condition such as `s IS NOT NULL` was meant to exclude. A query like `WHERE s IS NOT NULL AND strlen(s) > 1` can fail with a null error only after a plan change, which makes the bug intermittent and hard to trace. The supported defenses are to make the UDF null-aware itself, or to wrap the call so the guard is part of one expression, for example `CASE WHEN s IS NOT NULL THEN strlen(s) END`. Do not rely on filter placement, and do not assume that a passing test on one plan proves the order. The same rule applies to any side effect or exception in a UDF: validate inputs inside the function.

examPoints: Large or regular workloads should use built-in functions such as `regexp_extract`; a Python UDF is the choice for hard logic, ad hoc work and moderate data.

Repeated model loading per batch is fixed with an Iterator pandas UDF that initializes once; a UDF that works in a notebook but fails in a view on a dashboard points to a classic SQL warehouse, not to privileges.
Null errors that appear after a plan change come from unguaranteed evaluation order, fixed by null-aware UDFs or `CASE WHEN`; `STRICT ISOLATION` is for UDFs that run code or touch files and state.

quiz.q: A scalar `pd.Series -> pd.Series` UDF scores 800 million rows and loads a 600 MB model inside the function. Executors spend most time deserializing the model. Which design removes the repeated load?
choices: Increase the batch size so the same model is deserialized for fewer, larger rows
Convert the logic to a row-by-row Python UDF that caches the model in a global
An iterator pandas UDF that loads the model once before the loop
Add the `STRICT ISOLATION` characteristic so that each batch gets its own fresh isolated environment
quiz.explain: The iterator form receives all batches of a task in one call, so initialization before the loop happens once. A larger batch only reduces the count, a row-by-row UDF is slower, and strict isolation adds separate environments instead of sharing work.

quiz.q: A Unity Catalog Python UDF is used in a view. Dashboards on a classic SQL warehouse fail on the view, while a notebook cluster works. `EXECUTE` and `SELECT` are granted. What should the team do?
choices: Grant `USAGE` on every catalog in the workspace to the dashboard owner and viewers
Re-create the function as a built-in that skips the catalog and schema name
Run the dashboards on a serverless or pro SQL warehouse
Add `STRICT ISOLATION` to the function so the classic warehouse accepts it
quiz.explain: Views that contain Unity Catalog Python UDFs fail on classic SQL warehouses, so the compute type is the problem. Extra grants cannot fix it, built-ins cannot be re-created that way, and isolation only changes how the UDF runs.

days.recap: Prefer built-ins at scale, use iterator pandas UDFs to initialize once, remember that Unity Catalog Python UDFs depend on compute type and need EXECUTE, and never rely on predicate order to guard a UDF.

days.title: Lakeflow Pipelines with Auto Loader, and Structured Streaming versus Declarative Pipelines

concepts.heading: Auto Loader Discovery, Backfills and Restarts
concepts.body: The associate guide covers Auto Loader basics, so this day covers failure behavior. With `cloudFiles.useManagedFileEvents` set to `true`, the first run lists the whole load path to synchronize with the file events cache and stores a read position in the checkpoint. Later runs read new-file notifications and skip the listing. If a stream stays stopped for more than seven days, that read position expires and the next run does a full listing again: nothing is lost or duplicated, but the run is slow, so run such streams at least weekly. In classic file notification mode a file can still be missed, because cloud providers do not guarantee delivery of every event. A backfill is a periodic asynchronous listing that catches missed files, and it runs only if you set `cloudFiles.backfillInterval`, which has no default; with file events Databricks handles backfill itself, so do not set it. With the default `addNewColumns` schema evolution mode and no explicit schema, a new source column stops the stream with `UnknownFieldException` on purpose; the restart succeeds with the new schema, so run it as a Lakeflow Jobs task with retries instead of paging an operator.

concepts.heading: Streaming Tables, Refreshes and Append Flows
concepts.body: A streaming table processes each input record once and expects an append-only source. If an upstream Delta table gets updates or deletes, such as a GDPR purge, the stream fails by default. `skipChangeCommits` processes only appended rows and ignores the other commits, which fits when the deletion is handled separately in each layer. Refresh semantics matter most for history. A default refresh uses the stored checkpoint. A full refresh clears the table data and the flow checkpoints and reprocesses everything the source still has, so records already removed by a storage lifecycle rule or a short Kafka retention are dropped from the target. Setting the table property `pipelines.reset.allowed` to `false` blocks full refreshes. Resetting only the checkpoints of selected flows, through the pipeline update API, restarts reading without clearing the table. To add sources, use multiple append flows into one streaming table, each with its own checkpoint, and a one-time `ONCE` flow for a historical backfill, with no full refresh and no `UNION`.

concepts.heading: Pipeline Mode and Who Controls It
concepts.body: Pipeline mode is independent of the dataset type. A triggered update processes the data available when it starts and stops, so compute costs exist only during the update; it fits freshness of ten minutes, hourly or daily. A continuous pipeline keeps running and fits freshness of seconds to a few minutes but needs always-on compute. When a job orchestrates a pipeline, the job decides: a triggered or scheduled job runs one update and stops even if the pipeline mode says continuous, and a continuous job runs the pipeline continuously even if the mode is triggered. Databricks recommends running continuous pipelines as a continuous job and leaving the pipeline mode on triggered. For twenty-five tables with a thirty-minute freshness target and lowest cost, one triggered pipeline started every thirty minutes beats always-on queries. On serverless compute for jobs, `Trigger.ProcessingTime` and `Trigger.Continuous` are rejected with `INFINITE_STREAMING_TRIGGER_NOT_SUPPORTED`; use `Trigger.AvailableNow` or move the logic into a continuous serverless pipeline.

concepts.heading: Structured Streaming or Declarative Pipelines
concepts.body: A pipeline is a set of declared datasets (streaming tables, materialized views, views) and flows. The engine analyzes dependencies before running, plans the order, retries flows and manages checkpoints. That static planning explains the restrictions. `pivot()` has to read the data to learn the pivot values, so a pipeline rejects it; rewrite it with conditional aggregation such as `SUM(CASE WHEN metric = 'cpu' THEN value END)`. Each dataset can be defined only once across pipelines, except for append flows on a streaming table, so two teams writing the same table need one definition plus one flow per topic. Time travel queries work on streaming tables but not on materialized views. Arbitrary side effects inside dataset functions are not a supported design. When each micro-batch must write a table, call a REST service and run a `MERGE` over JDBC in one function, use Structured Streaming with `foreachBatch` as a Lakeflow Jobs task. When the work is declarative transformation and CDC, prefer the pipeline.

examPoints: Know Auto Loader recovery: stopped more than seven days with file events means a full listing, `cloudFiles.backfillInterval` is opt-in, and the default schema mode fails once on purpose and needs a retry.
Full refresh drops history the source no longer has; `pipelines.reset.allowed` protects it, and append flows or checkpoint resets add or restart sources without clearing the table.
The job's mode overrides the pipeline's, `pivot()` and duplicate dataset definitions are pipeline limits, and custom per-batch side effects belong to `foreachBatch`.

quiz.q: A streaming table `bronze_events` holds two years of history from JSON files, and a lifecycle rule deletes the source files after 30 days. A full refresh left only the last month. Which setting would have prevented it?
choices: Setting `cloudFiles.backfillInterval` to one year so older files are re-listed
Set the table property `pipelines.reset.allowed` to `false`
Switching the whole pipeline to continuous mode so that the stream never needs any refresh again
Setting `skipChangeCommits` on the stream so deleted files are never reprocessed
quiz.explain: A full refresh clears the table and reprocesses only files that still exist, so the property that blocks full refreshes protects the history. A backfill lists existing files only, continuous mode does not stop a manual refresh, and skipChangeCommits concerns upstream Delta commits.

quiz.q: A pipeline's mode is continuous, but operations wrap it in a job with an hourly schedule. How does it behave, and what is recommended for continuous processing?
choices: It runs continuously and the hourly schedule is ignored, so no other job setting is needed at all
The job takes precedence, so each run is one update; use a continuous job
The pipeline fails to start because a scheduled job cannot start a pipeline in continuous mode
The pipeline mode takes precedence, so the job only monitors updates it never starts
quiz.explain: When a job orchestrates a pipeline it decides the execution mode, so an hourly job gives one update per run. Databricks recommends a continuous job for continuous processing. The other choices reverse precedence or invent a failure.

days.recap: Auto Loader recovers through retries, backfills and weekly runs; a full refresh can destroy history; the job beats the pipeline mode; and Structured Streaming with foreachBatch handles custom side effects that declarative pipelines do not.

days.title: Streaming Table or Materialized View, and AUTO CDC for SCD Types 1 and 2

concepts.heading: Choosing the Dataset Type
concepts.body: A streaming table processes each input record once and keeps what it has ingested even if the source later loses it. A materialized view guarantees that its result equals the batch query over the current inputs, recomputing incrementally or fully as needed. Choose by the requirement. Bronze ingestion of files that a lifecycle rule archives after thirty days needs a streaming table, because history must outlive the source. A report that must show the current customer segment for all historical orders needs a materialized view, because a stream-static join in a streaming table joins each row once, with the dimension as it was then, and later dimension changes never touch written rows. A low-latency windowed aggregation of append-only events over the clock needs a streaming table with a watermark in a continuous pipeline; a materialized view recomputes its result on each update rather than emitting clock-driven windows. Changing a streaming table's query affects only new rows. To reprocess history, run a full refresh of only that table when its source still holds the complete history.

concepts.heading: Materialized View Refresh Behavior
concepts.body: A materialized view refreshes incrementally only on serverless pipelines; classic pipelines always recompute fully. Even on serverless, incremental refresh is cost-based and best effort: the engine may pick a full recompute, though the result is identical. Summing `FLOAT` or `DOUBLE` values gives order-dependent results, so the engine cannot update a previous aggregate incrementally and plans a full refresh. Casting the value to a decimal type makes incremental planning possible. Some incremental operations also need row tracking on the source tables, and a source recreated without it can silently push the view back to full recompute. The planning information in the pipeline event log shows why a refresh was full. A refresh policy makes the intent explicit. `AUTO` is cost-based, `INCREMENTAL` prefers incremental but may fall back, and `INCREMENTAL STRICT` requires incremental refresh and fails if that is not possible. Use the strict policy when an unexpected full refresh would break the SLA or budget and you would rather debug a failure.

concepts.heading: AUTO CDC Mechanics for SCD Type 1 and Type 2
concepts.body: `AUTO CDC` (formerly APPLY CHANGES) applies change events in the order of `sequence_by`, not arrival order. The column must be sortable, follow the true order of changes in the source, and be non-null; a log position or commit version works, while `current_timestamp()` added in the pipeline records processing time and lets old values overwrite newer ones. Delete events need a real sequence value too. In Type 1 the target keeps the latest values; an older event arriving late is ignored. In Type 2 the target stores versions with `__START_AT` and `__END_AT`: a change closes the current version and opens a new one, a delete closes the current version with the delete's sequence value, and active rows have `__END_AT IS NULL`. `track_history_except_column_list` stops a noisy column such as `last_seen_at` from creating new versions. For partial updates that send NULL for unchanged columns, `ignore_null_updates_column_list` protects only the listed columns, so NULL can still clear the others.

concepts.heading: Snapshots and Downstream Reads of CDC Targets
concepts.body: When a source offers no change log, only periodic full extracts, `AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT` compares consecutive snapshots, derives inserts, updates and deletes, and applies Type 1 or Type 2 logic. Snapshots must be processed in increasing version order, so a non-increasing version fails the update. Products absent from a newer snapshot are closed in Type 2, and two price changes between snapshots appear as one change because only the two states are visible. The target of an AUTO CDC flow is updated and deleted in place, so it is not an append-only source. A plain streaming read of it fails on commits that update or delete files, and `skipChangeCommits` cannot be used when the source is the target of an AUTO CDC flow. The correct downstream dataset is a materialized view over the target, which recomputes, incrementally where supported, whenever the target changes. For comparison, a hand-written `MERGE` in `foreachBatch` must handle duplicates in a batch, late events and deletes by itself; AUTO CDC removes that code.

examPoints: Streaming table for history and per-row-once logic, materialized view for results that must match current inputs; do not enrich with a mutable dimension inside a streaming table when history must reflect new values.
Incremental materialized view refresh needs serverless, decimal instead of DOUBLE sums and row tracking where required; `INCREMENTAL STRICT` makes a silent full refresh fail loudly.
AUTO CDC needs a non-null `sequence_by` that follows source order, Type 2 closes versions with `__END_AT`, and a downstream aggregate of a CDC target is a materialized view.

quiz.q: An AUTO CDC flow applies a Debezium topic with `sequence_by = F.current_timestamp()` added upstream. Messages from different partitions arrive out of order and old values sometimes replace newer ones. What is the root cause and fix?
choices: Sequence follows processing time; use a source commit position as `sequence_by`
The flow is set to Type 1, so switch to Type 2 and every late event is kept in order
The pipeline is in triggered mode, so switch to continuous and arrival order becomes reliable
The key columns are missing, so add all columns as keys to let the flow sort the events
quiz.explain: AUTO CDC compares sequence values, and processing time does not reflect the order of changes in the source. Switching Type or mode does not repair a wrong ordering column, and adding keys changes row identity, not ordering.

quiz.q: A silver table is an AUTO CDC Type 1 target with upserts and deletes. A gold dataset must always match the active-customer count per region. Which definition is correct?
choices: A streaming table that reads silver with `skipChangeCommits` and counts the appended rows only
A materialized view that aggregates silver and is recomputed when silver changes
A streaming table that reads silver with `delta.appendOnly` enabled on the source
A streaming table with a watermark on the silver update time and an append output
quiz.explain: The CDC target is changed in place, so downstream aggregates must be recomputed from its current state. Ignoring change commits is not allowed on an AUTO CDC target and would lose updates and deletes, and an append-only property forbids the updates and deletes that the target needs.

days.recap: Streaming tables keep history, materialized views track current inputs, refresh policies control incremental behavior, and AUTO CDC depends on a correct non-null sequence column.

days.title: Lakeflow Jobs: UI, API and CLI, Control Flow, and Compute Choices

concepts.heading: Creating, Changing and Starting Jobs Programmatically
concepts.body: The Databricks CLI wraps the Jobs REST API, so each command maps to a request. The classic trap is `reset` versus `update`. `jobs reset` overwrites all settings of the job with the supplied definition, so a file containing only a `schedule` removes the tasks and cluster settings and the next run fails. `jobs update` adds, changes or removes specific settings and leaves the rest. Starting a run has three paths. A schedule or trigger starts it from the definition, `run-now` starts an existing job, and `submit` takes a definition and triggers a one-time run: the job is not saved, does not appear in the Jobs UI, and does not retry on failure. Because it is not saved, serverless compute cannot be auto-optimized after failures, so explicit classic settings may suit a one-off integration check. For an external scheduler that retries on timeouts, `run-now` accepts an `idempotency_token` of up to 64 characters; reusing the token returns the existing run, so exactly one run is launched.

concepts.heading: Parameters Reach Tasks in Two Styles
concepts.body: Tasks take parameters in two forms. Key-value tasks (notebook, SQL, Run Job, and Python wheel keyword arguments) receive job parameters automatically, and if a task parameter has the same key as a job parameter, the job parameter wins. Tasks that take a JSON array of strings (Python script, Python wheel positional arguments, JAR, Spark Submit and For each) receive only what the array contains, as if run from a command line. A Python script that expects `run_date` must therefore have `{{job.parameters.run_date}}` written into its array. Task values pass small scalar results between tasks, such as a count or a path, and a task reads them with `{{tasks.<name>.values.<key>}}`. An If/else condition task compares two operands: `==` and `!=` compare as strings, while `>`, `>=`, `<` and `<=` compare numerically. Only numeric, string and boolean task values are allowed, so a Python list makes the condition fail; set a scalar such as a bad-record count and compare it with `> 0`.

concepts.heading: Run If, For Each and Repair
concepts.body: The Run if setting decides whether a task runs given the outcome of its dependencies. A task whose Run if condition is not met is Excluded, for example with At least one failed. An Excluded upstream task counts as successful for dependants, and if all dependencies of a task are Excluded the task is Excluded too, whatever its own Run if says, cascading down a chain. To have a final report run every night, make it depend on the main task as well and set Run if to All done. A For each task runs a nested task once per element of an input array. Concurrency defaults to 1, so 150 four-minute iterations take ten hours until you raise it, a capacity decision for compute and sources. The nested task cannot be another For each task; flatten a cross product into one array of objects read as `{{input.region}}`. For long lists, build the array in an upstream task and reference its task value. Repair re-runs only unsuccessful tasks and their dependants, and works only for jobs with two or more tasks.

concepts.heading: Compute and Environment Choices for Tasks
concepts.body: Databricks recommends serverless compute for most automated workloads: fewer settings, fast start-up and automatic scaling. Classic jobs compute is for non-SQL tasks that need what serverless does not offer, such as compute-scoped init scripts that install an operating system package, or compute policies. Serverless installs Python packages through the environment, a base environment plus a dependency list. It also rejects some APIs: `df.checkpoint()`, `spark.catalog.cacheTable()` and `CACHE TABLE` raise exceptions, while `df.cache()` and `df.persist()` work; replace a checkpoint with a write to a Delta table. Global temporary views are not supported, so tasks that exchange data should share a table, since each task runs in an isolated environment. For streaming, only triggers that end on their own run on serverless jobs, so an always-on query with a short processing interval belongs in a continuous serverless pipeline. A heavy classic pipeline that hits out-of-memory on skewed batches can move to serverless, which adds vertical autoscaling on top of horizontal.

examPoints: `jobs reset` overwrites the whole definition and `jobs update` patches; `run-now` with an `idempotency_token` prevents duplicate runs, and `submit` is an unsaved one-time run without retries.
Python script tasks need job parameters written into the JSON array, If/else accepts only scalar task values, and Excluded tasks cascade through Run if conditions.
Serverless is the default, classic compute is for init scripts and custom settings, and serverless limits include triggers, `checkpoint()`, `cacheTable()` and global temporary views.

quiz.q: A CI step updates a job from a JSON file that contains only the new `schedule` block using `databricks jobs reset`. Afterward the job has no tasks. What is the right approach for partial changes?
choices: Use `databricks jobs submit` so the schedule is added without touching the saved job
Reset overwrites all settings, so partial changes use `databricks jobs update`
Add `max_concurrent_runs` to the file so reset keeps the existing task settings
Use `run-now` with an `idempotency_token` so that the saved job gets the new schedule applied
quiz.explain: `reset` replaces everything missing from the file, while `update` changes only the specified settings. `submit` creates an unsaved one-time run, concurrency settings do not preserve tasks, and `run-now` starts runs rather than editing the job.

quiz.q: A job has `process`, then `cleanup` (Run if At least one failed), then `report` depending only on `cleanup`. On successful nights `report` does not run. What is the right change?
choices: Set Run if All succeeded on `cleanup` so the report follows it every night
Make `report` depend on `process` too, with Run if All done
Enable repair on the job so skipped tasks are re-run when the night ends
Move `report` into a For each task with concurrency greater than 1 over the main task
quiz.explain: When every dependency of a task is Excluded, the task is Excluded regardless of its own Run if. Depending on `process` as well, with All done, makes the report run whatever happens. Repair is for failed runs and For each does not change dependency evaluation.

days.recap: Know reset versus update, the three ways to start a run, idempotency tokens, how parameters reach each task type, how Excluded cascades, and which serverless limits push work to classic compute or a pipeline.

days.title: Testing Pipeline Code and Stateful Structured Streaming

concepts.heading: Testable Pipeline Code
concepts.body: Databricks recommends keeping Python functions and their tests outside notebooks: import functions from a module in a Git folder or a bundle source folder and test them with `pytest`. Separate logic from I/O. A transformation is a pure function from DataFrame to DataFrame, covered by unit tests with a handful of in-memory rows, while a thin entry point reads and writes the real tables. Tests should use fake data, never production tables, particularly for code that changes data. Two ways to run Spark exist in tests. Local PySpark gives fast unit tests on a laptop or CI runner with no workspace. Databricks Connect runs code on remote compute through Spark Connect and suits integration tests that must read Unity Catalog tables or run on the real runtime. The two conflict: `databricks-connect` ships its own `pyspark` module, so an image built with both fails with Spark session errors. Uninstall the standalone PySpark in the Connect environment and run local unit tests in a separate environment.

concepts.heading: Comparing DataFrames Correctly
concepts.body: A test such as `actual.collect() == expected.collect()` is brittle. Spark gives no ordering guarantee after a shuffle, and floating-point aggregates can differ in the last digits when values are added in a different order. `assertDataFrameEqual` from `pyspark.testing` compares schema and rows, ignores row order by default, and compares numeric values with a relative and absolute tolerance. Schema is part of equality. Column types must match unless `ignoreColumnType=True`, nullability is ignored by default, and column order matters unless `ignoreColumnOrder=True`. A common trap: `createDataFrame` from Python tuples infers integers as `LongType`, while a function that casts to `int` returns `IntegerType`. Values print identically and the assertion fails. Declare an explicit schema for the expected DataFrame instead of loosening the check, so the test also guards the output contract.

concepts.heading: Watermarks, Output Modes and State
concepts.body: A watermark is the maximum event time seen minus the threshold, set at the start of each trigger. Data less than the threshold behind the latest data is guaranteed to be aggregated; data later than that is not guaranteed to be dropped, so the guarantee is strict in one direction only. Append mode writes a window once, after the watermark passes its end, so every result is delayed by the threshold. Update mode writes changed rows as soon as they change, so a dashboard sees partial totals early, and state is still dropped after the watermark. Complete mode rewrites the whole result and never drops aggregation state. With several watermarked inputs the global watermark defaults to the `min` policy, the slowest stream, which keeps late data but holds state longer; `multipleWatermarkPolicy` set to `max` follows the fastest and risks dropping the slower feed's records. Stream-stream joins support append mode only. Outer joins need watermarks plus an event-time range condition, and unmatched rows are emitted with NULLs after the watermark passes.

concepts.heading: foreachBatch, Checkpoints and Recovery
concepts.body: `foreachBatch` gives at-least-once guarantees. The checkpoint's offset log records a planned batch before it runs and the commit log records it afterwards, so a failure between two writes replays the same batch with the same `batchId`. For Delta writes, set `txnAppId` and `txnVersion` bound to `batchId` so a replayed write is skipped, and let errors propagate so the job retries the whole batch. A batch that has an offset entry but no commit is re-planned with exactly the same offsets. Lowering `maxFilesPerTrigger` after an out-of-memory failure therefore applies only to later batches; the first replayed batch needs more compute. With a stateful operator such as `dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark`, the function must consume the whole batch DataFrame, even on a skip path. Reading part of it with `limit`, `show(2)` or an early `return` leaves state inconsistent and the next batch fails.

examPoints: Unit tests use local PySpark and pure DataFrame functions; integration tests use Databricks Connect, and the two packages conflict in one environment.
Use `assertDataFrameEqual` with an explicit expected schema, and remember the watermark guarantee is one-directional; update mode lowers latency, append mode waits for the watermark.
foreachBatch is at-least-once: use `txnAppId` and `txnVersion` for idempotence, expect replays to reuse old offsets, and always consume the whole batch with stateful operators.

quiz.q: A unit test builds the expected DataFrame with `createDataFrame([(1, 'a'), (2, 'b')], ['id', 'code'])`. The function under test returns `id` cast to `int`. The values look identical but `assertDataFrameEqual` fails. What is the cause and the fix?
choices: Row order differs after the shuffle, so set `checkRowOrder=True` on the comparison
Nullability differs, so set `ignoreNullable=False` to let the check pass for both frames
Inferred `LongType` differs from `IntegerType`; declare the expected schema
The tolerance is too tight, so raise `rtol` until the integer columns compare equal
quiz.explain: Schema is part of equality, and inferred Python integers are 64-bit while a cast to `int` is 32-bit. An explicit expected schema fixes the test honestly. Row order is ignored by default, nullability is ignored by default, and tolerances do not apply to type mismatches.

quiz.q: A `foreachBatch` function appends each micro-batch to `silver.orders` then to `silver.orders_audit`. After a failure between the writes and a job retry, `silver.orders` holds the batch twice. Which change gives the strongest guarantee?
choices: Write both tables with `txnAppId` and `txnVersion` bound to `batchId`
Wrap each write in a `try/except` that swallows the error so that the checkpoint commits the whole batch
Lower `maxFilesPerTrigger` so each batch contains too few rows to be written twice
Switch the stream to complete output mode so every batch overwrites the earlier rows
quiz.explain: A replayed batch keeps its `batchId`, so idempotent Delta writes skip data that was already committed. Swallowing errors commits a half-written batch, the trigger limit does not stop replays, and output mode does not govern a custom foreachBatch sink.

days.recap: Test pure functions with pytest and explicit schemas, keep Connect and PySpark apart, choose output modes by latency versus completeness, and make foreachBatch writes idempotent with txnAppId and txnVersion.

days.title: Ingesting from Message Buses and Cloud Storage, and Applying Changes Incrementally

concepts.heading: Kafka Offsets, Checkpoints and Poison Messages
concepts.body: The Kafka source returns key and value as binary plus topic, partition, offset and timestamp, so deserialization is your job with from_avro, from_json or from_protobuf. The startingOffsets option only decides where a new query starts. A restarted query resumes from the offsets in its checkpoint and ignores the option, so switching latest to earliest on a running query does not backfill anything. To recover a gap, start a second bounded query with its own checkpoint, explicit starting offsets at the start of the gap and an AvailableNow trigger, and write idempotently so overlap with the live stream causes no duplicates. Changing the subscribed topics, the number or type of sources, or the schema of stateful operations is not supported on the same checkpoint, while filters and rate limits can be edited. from_avro defaults to FAILFAST, so one corrupt payload fails the batch again after every restart. In PERMISSIVE mode corrupt records become NULL, and rows with a NULL result but a non-NULL value go to a dead-letter table with topic, partition and offset.

concepts.heading: Kinesis and Pub/Sub Delivery Semantics
concepts.body: Each Kinesis shard supports a fixed number of GetRecords calls per second, shared by every polling reader. Several queries reading one stream in polling mode therefore see ReadProvisionedThroughputExceeded and a rising iterator age, and a larger cluster does not help because the limit sits on the shard. Databricks advises that a query be the only consumer of a stream. When several queries each need all records, use enhanced fan-out, which gives every registered consumer dedicated throughput per shard. A registered consumer adds Kinesis charges, so set requireConsumerDeregistration to true or manage consumers yourself. Specify either streamName or streamARN, never both, and do not switch between them on an active query, because Databricks does not support the switch and restarting can duplicate or lose records, so cut over with a new query, a fresh checkpoint and an idempotent sink. The Pub/Sub connector has exactly-once semantics only for rows it receives from the subscriber. Pub/Sub can still publish duplicates when producers retry, and each copy gets its own messageId, so deduplicate on a business key such as event_id after setting a watermark, using dropDuplicatesWithinWatermark.

concepts.heading: Cloud Storage Formats and Hidden Files with Auto Loader
concepts.body: Auto Loader handles JSON, CSV, XML, Parquet, Avro, ORC, text and binary files, with schema inference and evolution. XML has no inherent record boundary, so the rowTag option is required and names the element that is read as one row. For a file shaped as orders containing many order elements, rowTag is order. Using the root element would give one row per file holding an array of orders. File sources also skip hidden names: ignoredPathSegmentRegex defaults to ^[._] and is matched against each directory and file name below the path being read, so a partner file named _2026-11-01_orders.csv is listed in storage but never ingested, and a directory whose name matches excludes its whole subtree. The fix is to rename the file or change the regex. Setting an empty string disables the filter, and then marker files such as _SUCCESS can be read too, so a more precise pattern is safer. These behaviors explain most reports of files that exist but never arrive, and they are checked before suspecting notifications, permissions or the checkpoint.

concepts.heading: Applying Change Feeds and Snapshots to Delta and Iceberg Readers
concepts.body: Change events arrive late, out of order and duplicated, so apply them by a sequence, not by arrival. AUTO CDC takes a key, a SEQUENCE BY column and SCD type 1 or 2, and SEQUENCE BY STRUCT(event_ts, event_id) breaks ties on the second field. With hand-written MERGE, the source must have at most one row per target row or the statement fails, so a micro-batch reading the change data feed should drop update_preimage rows, keep the highest _commit_version per key and use a delete clause for _change_type delete. An at-least-once log source is deduplicated inside the batch, then merged insert-only with a predicate on the partition column, such as the last seven days, so the merge prunes files. For nightly snapshots without change flags, one MERGE combines WHEN MATCHED AND changed, WHEN NOT MATCHED and WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE DELETE. The change data feed is transient: old versions disappear with log cleanup and VACUUM, so a stale startingVersion fails and the target must be rebuilt from a snapshot. For Iceberg readers of a Delta target, UniForm needs column mapping, and deletion vectors must be purged with REORG first.

examPoints: A question about a Kafka backfill after changing startingOffsets is testing that the option applies only to a new query, so the answer is a separate bounded query with its own checkpoint and an idempotent sink.
A question about throttling with several Kinesis readers is testing enhanced fan-out, and a question about Pub/Sub duplicates is testing deduplication on a business key within a watermark.
A question on out-of-order or repeated CDC events is testing a sequence column with a tie-break in AUTO CDC, or one source row per key in MERGE, and the transient nature of the change data feed.

quiz.q: A Kafka stream started with startingOffsets set to latest and a checkpoint lost two days of events to a parsing bug. An engineer changes the option to earliest and restarts the same query, but the gap is not filled. What should be done?
choices: Run a bounded query with a new checkpoint and offsets at the gap start, writing idempotently
Delete the checkpoint folder of the live query and restart it with earliest, so all retained topic history replays into the table
Keep the checkpoint and set failOnDataLoss to false, which makes the running query reread the gap automatically
Raise the trigger interval of the live query, because a longer interval lets it catch up on the skipped offsets
quiz.explain: startingOffsets is read only when a query starts without a checkpoint, so the restart resumed from the recorded offsets. A separate bounded query with its own checkpoint reads just the gap, and an idempotent write avoids duplicates. Deleting the checkpoint replays everything and duplicates rows.

quiz.q: A CDC feed delivers events for the same customer out of order, and two events can share one event_ts but have increasing event_id values. A pipeline must keep the newest state per customer without history. Which AUTO CDC configuration fits?
choices: Keys on customer_id, SCD type 2, and SEQUENCE BY event_ts alone, with ties resolved by arrival order
Keys on customer_id, SCD type 1, and SEQUENCE BY STRUCT(event_ts, event_id)
Keys on event_id, SCD type 1, and SEQUENCE BY customer_id so every event becomes its own row
No sequence column, because AUTO CDC applies events in the order the micro-batches arrive
quiz.explain: Type 1 keeps only the latest row per key, and a STRUCT sequence orders by event_ts first and event_id on ties. Type 2 would keep history, and ordering by arrival gives wrong results for late events.

days.recap: Kafka startingOffsets applies only to a new query, so backfill with a separate bounded query and checkpoint; FAILFAST poison messages need PERMISSIVE plus a dead-letter table. Kinesis needs enhanced fan-out for several readers, Pub/Sub needs business-key deduplication, Auto Loader needs rowTag and an eye on hidden-name filters. CDC is applied by sequence, not arrival, and the change data feed is transient.

days.title: Lakeflow Connect CDC from Relational Databases: Gateway, Source Setup and Failure Recovery

concepts.heading: Gateway and Pipeline: Two Components, Two Modes
concepts.body: A gateway-based database connector, such as the SQL Server connector, has two parts with different rules. The ingestion gateway extracts snapshots and change logs from the source. It runs on classic compute and must stay in continuous mode, because the source keeps its logs only for a retention period and a stopped gateway lets changes expire. Do not stop it manually. Each start also provisions a virtual machine, so restarts are slow. The ingestion pipeline applies the extracted changes to the destination streaming tables and runs on serverless compute, and continuous mode is not supported for it. It is run on a schedule or triggered, and Databricks recommends at least five minutes between runs because serverless startup takes time. This split gives a cost design for a few minutes of freshness: keep the gateway running and schedule the pipeline every few minutes, instead of paying for a continuously running pipeline. Databricks tracks what was extracted and applied, so a failed run resumes at that point without data loss, but only while the logs still exist on the source. If they expired, the affected tables need a full refresh.

concepts.heading: Preparing the Source: Change Tracking, CDC and Keys
concepts.body: The connector reads a change feed that SQL Server itself maintains, so the source is prepared before any pipeline runs. Change tracking records that a row changed, not the sequence of operations, requires a primary key and adds little load. Change data capture records every operation and keeps a history. Databricks recommends change tracking for any table with a primary key to minimize load on the source, and if both are enabled the connector uses change tracking. A managed connector must apply updates and deletes, so it needs a key for every table. It uses the primary key first, then a unique key or unique index, and otherwise treats all columns except large objects as a bundled key. Rows that are identical in all of those columns are ingested as a single row, so a table such as audit_events with true duplicates loses rows in the destination. The repair is a surrogate unique key or unique index on the source, then a refresh of that table. Choose CDC instead when a table has no primary key and a unique index can not be added, accepting higher source overhead.

concepts.heading: Availability Groups and Failover
concepts.body: How the change feed behaves after a source failover decides whether ingestion resumes cleanly. With change tracking, the tracking data is not replicated to secondary nodes, so any change of source node, including an Availability Group failover, requires a full refresh of all tables in the pipeline. With CDC, the log sequence number checkpoints are portable across replicas. If the connector connects through the Availability Group listener address, the pipeline can resume after an unplanned failover without data loss. So the setting that must survive failovers favors CDC through the listener, even though change tracking is lighter for single-node sources. The documented resume path is the listener address, and only primary instances are supported as a source. The same logic applies to maintenance: anything that interrupts the gateway for longer than the source log retention, or moves the source to a new node under change tracking, ends in a full refresh. Exam wording like unplanned failover, without a full refresh of all tables points at CDC with the listener; wording like lowest overhead with primary keys points at change tracking.

concepts.heading: Schema Changes, Dropped Tables and Who Can Set It Up
concepts.body: Database connectors handle schema changes in a defined way. A new column is picked up on the next pipeline run unless you opt out, and new tables appear if you ingest a whole schema. A column deleted at the source is not dropped in the destination. A table property marks it inactive so history stays queryable, and if a different column later appears with the same name, the pipeline fails on that table until you drop the inactive column manually or run a full refresh. Renames and data type changes need a refresh as well. When a source table is deleted, the destination table is not deleted either. You drop it manually, which differs from Spark Declarative Pipelines, where removing a dataset from the code removes it from the pipeline objects. For setup there are two models. In the single-user model an admin does everything. In the multi-user model an admin prepares the source with a dedicated ingestion user and creates a Unity Catalog connection that stores the credential, and non-admin engineers use it to create gateway-pipeline pairs without ever seeing the password.

examPoints: A question about freshness of a few minutes at lowest cost is testing a continuously running gateway on classic compute with a short schedule for the serverless ingestion pipeline.
A question about change tracking versus CDC is testing primary keys and source load, and one about unplanned Availability Group failover is testing CDC through the listener.
A question about a gateway stopped longer than log retention is testing that changes are gone and a full refresh is required, and one about identical rows is testing the key the connector picks.

quiz.q: A product team wants SQL Server changes in Delta tables within a few minutes at the lowest cost that still meets this. An engineer proposes switching the ingestion pipeline to continuous mode and stopping the gateway overnight. Which design is right?
choices: Run the ingestion pipeline continuously and schedule the gateway every few minutes, since pipelines read the logs
Stop the gateway overnight, run the pipeline continuously, and restart the gateway each morning to save cost
Keep the gateway running on classic compute and schedule the serverless pipeline every few minutes
Replace the gateway with a nightly full refresh of all tables, which avoids depending on source log retention
quiz.explain: The gateway must stay continuous so changes are not lost to source log retention, and it runs on classic compute. The ingestion pipeline applies staged changes and is scheduled. Stopping the gateway risks expired logs and a full refresh.

quiz.q: A company runs SQL Server in an Availability Group. After an unplanned failover, ingestion must resume without a full refresh of all tables. Which setup gives that?
choices: Change tracking on all tables, connecting to the primary replica by its own host name
Either feed works, because the gateway rebuilds the change history after any failover
Change tracking, because its data is replicated to secondary nodes automatically
Change data capture, connecting through the Availability Group listener address
quiz.explain: CDC log sequence checkpoints are portable across replicas, and the listener address lets the pipeline resume. Change tracking data is not replicated to secondaries, so a node change forces a full refresh of all tables.

days.recap: Gateway on classic compute, always continuous; ingestion pipeline serverless, scheduled. Change tracking is light and needs primary keys; CDC survives Availability Group failover through the listener. Expired source logs mean a full refresh. Dropped columns turn inactive, dropped source tables stay in the destination, and a Unity Catalog connection lets non-admins create pairs.

days.title: OpenSharing, Clean Rooms and Lakehouse Federation with Governance

concepts.heading: Choosing the OpenSharing Protocol
concepts.body: OpenSharing (called Delta Sharing in older docs) has two protocols, both served by the OpenSharing server built into Databricks. Databricks-to-Databricks shares data and AI assets with recipients that have a Unity Catalog-enabled workspace. It adds notebook sharing, volume sharing, model sharing, Unity Catalog governance, auditing and usage tracking on both sides, and works across accounts, clouds and regions. Databricks-to-Open shares tabular data with users on any platform, such as Power BI or Python, without a workspace. So a partner who needs a table, a volume of PDF files and a notebook must be a Databricks-to-Databricks recipient. For Databricks-to-Open recipients the provider chooses the authentication. A bearer token is a long-lived credential file the recipient must store securely, while OIDC federation lets the recipient identity provider issue short-lived tokens that Databricks validates, which suits security teams that reject stored long-lived tokens. On the consuming side of a Databricks-to-Databricks share, granting access is not enough: a metastore admin or privileged user must create a catalog from the share, and then analysts get ordinary Unity Catalog privileges on it.

concepts.heading: Share Versus Clean Room
concepts.body: A normal share gives the recipient read access to the provider data, so the recipient sees the rows and can run any code on them. It fits distribution. A clean room fits two or more parties that must combine sensitive data without direct access to each other raw records, such as an advertiser and a retailer computing customer overlap and conversion per campaign. Each party shares tables with the central clean room, an isolated Databricks-managed environment, using OpenSharing, and approved notebook code runs there on serverless compute. Collaborators review and approve the code before it touches the data. Safeguards matter for the exam. After creation a clean room is locked down, so no new collaborators can join, and a third company means creating a new clean room with all three. Each clean room is limited to ten collaborators. Because the code runs on serverless compute, data in a storage-firewalled bucket cannot be reached by default. Options are default storage, allowing the serverless compute in the network rules, or enabling SecureConnect for the clean room so firewalled storage is reachable without allowlisting that network.

concepts.heading: Lakehouse Federation: Query and Catalog Federation
concepts.body: Lakehouse Federation exposes external systems as Unity Catalog foreign catalogs. A connection stores the path and credentials, and a foreign catalog mirrors the external database. There are two kinds. Query federation targets relational databases such as MySQL, PostgreSQL and SQL Server through JDBC, with pushdown so the query runs partly in the remote system and partly in Databricks. It is read-only and suits ad hoc reporting and proofs of concept. Which operators go remote is a documented list per source: for PostgreSQL filters, projections, limits and aggregates are pushed down, but a window function runs on Databricks compute. Catalog federation connects external catalog platforms such as Hive Metastore or AWS Glue, and queries read the files directly in object storage and run only on Databricks compute, using a connection, a storage credential and an external location. That is the fast path to query Glue-registered tables from Unity Catalog during a staged migration. Neither kind writes: an INSERT into a foreign catalog fails, so publishing results to PostgreSQL needs a JDBC write in a job or another tool.

concepts.heading: Governing Federated Access and When to Ingest Instead
concepts.body: Federated access has two layers that must both allow a query. Unity Catalog privileges on the foreign catalog, schema and table decide which Databricks principals may query. The connection uses one shared database login, so that login decides what can be read at all, and end users never use their own database logins. Finance can therefore be granted only the ledger schema and marketing only another schema with ordinary grants on one foreign catalog, but if the database user lacks rights on a schema, a Unity Catalog SELECT still ends in a permission error that originates in the source. Dedicated access mode compute has an exception: you must own the underlying connection to query the foreign catalog, and CREATE FOREIGN CATALOG on it is not enough, while standard access mode and serverless use normal privileges. Federation sends every query to the source, so a growing operational dashboard loads the production database. When concurrency and volume grow and the source supports it, ingest with a Lakeflow Connect managed connector into Delta tables and point the dashboard at them.

examPoints: A question sharing tables, volumes and notebooks with a partner is testing Databricks-to-Databricks, and one with a vendor without a workspace that bans long-lived tokens is testing Databricks-to-Open with OIDC federation.
A question where neither party may see raw records and both review code is testing a clean room; a third collaborator later means a new clean room, and firewalled storage means SecureConnect.
A question on slow dashboards over a foreign catalog is testing ingestion with Lakeflow Connect, and one on INSERT into a foreign catalog is testing that federation is read-only.

quiz.q: A retailer wants to give a logistics partner a Unity Catalog table, a volume of PDF delivery notes and an explanatory notebook. The partner has its own Unity Catalog-enabled Databricks workspace. Which sharing approach fits?
choices: Databricks-to-Open with a bearer token, because tokens can carry any asset type and format
Databricks-to-Databricks, since notebooks and volumes need a Unity Catalog recipient
Export the files to a bucket and share the table through a view in a clean room
A foreign catalog on the partner side, which federates the retailer's volumes and notebooks
quiz.explain: Notebook and volume sharing are supported only by the Databricks-to-Databricks protocol with a Unity Catalog-enabled recipient. Databricks-to-Open shares tabular data, and a foreign catalog is read-only federation of external databases, not a sharing mechanism.

quiz.q: A federated PostgreSQL query filters orders to one month, sums amount per customer, then ranks customers with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY SUM(amount) DESC). Which statement describes where the work happens?
choices: Filter and aggregate go to PostgreSQL, while the window function runs on Databricks
Nothing is pushed down, since foreign catalogs always copy tables to Delta before querying
The window function is pushed down, while the filter and the aggregate run on Databricks compute
Everything is pushed down because query federation runs the whole statement inside PostgreSQL
quiz.explain: Query federation pushes down only a documented list of operators. Filters, projections and aggregates are on the list for PostgreSQL, while window functions are not, so ranking runs on Databricks compute.

days.recap: Databricks-to-Databricks carries notebooks, volumes and models; Databricks-to-Open serves any platform, with OIDC for short-lived tokens. Clean rooms combine data without exposing rows, are locked after creation and need SecureConnect for firewalled storage. Federation is read-only, governed by Unity Catalog grants plus the shared database login, and heavy dashboards should use ingested Delta tables.

days.title: Advanced Spark SQL and PySpark: Window Frames, Grouping Analytics, Joins and Approximate Aggregates

concepts.heading: Window Frames: Defaults, Ties and Forward Fill
concepts.body: A window function computes a value per row from a frame of related rows without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY does. PARTITION BY isolates groups, ORDER BY sequences them, and the frame limits which rows are visible. When the window has an ORDER BY and no explicit frame, the default is RANGE from unbounded preceding to the current row, and rows with equal ordering values are peers that fall into the frame together. Two consequences follow. First, last_value over that default frame returns the current row, or the last of its ties, so showing the final status of an order on every row needs ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING. Second, a running SUM ordered by a timestamp with ties gives tied rows the same total, and switching to ROWS makes each row a step but leaves the order among ties undefined, so totals can change between runs. Add a unique tie-breaker to ORDER BY. Forward fill of sparse sensor data uses last(temp, true) over PARTITION BY device_id ORDER BY ts ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW, where true ignores NULLs, with no self-join.

concepts.heading: Ranking, QUALIFY and Top-N Inside Aggregates
concepts.body: Ranking functions treat ties differently. For revenues 100, 100, 90, 80, 70 in descending order, row_number gives 1 to 5 and splits ties arbitrarily, rank gives 1, 1, 3, 4, 5 and skips numbers, dense_rank gives 1, 1, 2, 3, 4, and ntile(3) buckets rows by position, not by value. So the three highest distinct revenue values per category, with ties kept, is dense_rank less than or equal to 3. QUALIFY filters on window results without a wrapping subquery: SELECT ... QUALIFY dense_rank() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) <= 3. When the requirement is one row per key holding the latest N values as an array, with no window function and no self-join, max_by(expr, ordExpr, limit) in a plain GROUP BY returns an ARRAY of up to limit values from the rows with the largest ordering values; limit is an INT from 1 to 100,000, rows with a NULL ordering value are excluded, and ties on the cutoff make the result non-deterministic.

concepts.heading: Grouping Analytics and Join Semantics
concepts.body: ROLLUP, CUBE and GROUPING SETS compute several aggregation levels in one pass. In a subtotal row the rolled-up column shows NULL, which looks identical to a source NULL, so a row with region EU and channel NULL is ambiguous. Select grouping(channel), which is 1 when the column was aggregated away and 0 for real values including NULL, or grouping_id for several columns. For joins, an outer join keeps unmatched left rows with NULLs on the right, and a WHERE predicate such as x.year = 2026 runs after the join and is never true for NULL, so unmatched stores vanish and the LEFT JOIN behaves like an inner join. A condition that restricts the right table belongs in the ON clause, while WHERE suits conditions on the final result. Range joins match a value to an interval and can use binning. If the condition also has an equality on a numeric column, the optimizer may bin that column too and lose performance, so cast numeric equality keys to STRING on both sides so only the range condition is optimized.

concepts.heading: Approximate Aggregates at Scale
concepts.body: Distinct counts are not additive: a user active on Monday and Tuesday counts once for the week but once per day in the daily numbers, so summing stored daily counts overstates weekly uniques, exact or approximate. The fix is to store a mergeable sketch. hll_sketch_agg builds a HyperLogLog sketch as a compact BINARY value suitable for a table column, hll_union_agg merges the sketches of several days, and hll_sketch_estimate returns the approximate distinct count of the union. The error depends on lgConfigK, from 4 to 21 with default 12, and sketches to be merged need compatible settings. For percentiles over billions of rows, exact percentile needs every value of the group and gets costly at that size. approx_percentile(expr, percentile, accuracy) avoids sorting everything: accuracy is a positive integer defaulting to 10000, higher values cost more memory, and 1.0 divided by accuracy is the relative error. Accuracy 100 means about 1 percent error, 1000 about 0.1 percent, and the default about 0.01 percent. A target of 0.02 percent therefore needs at least 5000, and the default meets it.

examPoints: A question where last_value returns the current row is testing the default RANGE frame with ORDER BY, fixed with an explicit ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING frame.
A question about the top three distinct values with ties is testing dense_rank with QUALIFY, and one about the latest N values as an array per key is testing max_by with a limit.
A question about weekly uniques from daily counts is testing HyperLogLog sketches with hll_union_agg, and one on a LEFT JOIN losing rows is testing ON versus WHERE.

quiz.q: A report uses GROUP BY ROLLUP(region, channel) and shows a row with region EU and channel NULL. Analysts disagree whether it is a subtotal or EU sales with no channel recorded, because the source also contains NULL channels. How should the query separate the cases?
choices: Use CUBE instead of ROLLUP, because CUBE never reports NULL in subtotal rows
Replace NULL channels with a text value before the ROLLUP, so subtotal NULLs stay unique
Filter the output with WHERE channel IS NULL, which keeps only the subtotal rows
Select grouping(channel): 1 for rolled-up rows, 0 for real values including NULL
quiz.explain: grouping() distinguishes a rolled-up column from a source NULL. Replacing NULLs first merges real unknowns into one label, which changes the data, and CUBE also reports NULL for aggregated columns.

quiz.q: A daily job stores COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) per site and day over billions of events. Product now needs weekly and monthly unique users per site, and summing the daily counts overstates the result. What is the best design?
choices: Sum the stored daily approx_count_distinct values, which become exact once added across a week
Recompute COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) from the raw events for every weekly and monthly query, with no stored state
Store hll_sketch_agg(user_id) per site and day, then merge the period with hll_union_agg and estimate
Store the daily counts in a materialized view, since the view merges overlapping users
quiz.explain: Distinct counts do not add up. Mergeable HyperLogLog sketches stored per day can be unioned for any period and estimated. Recomputing from raw events works but is costly, and a view over counts cannot know which users overlap.

days.recap: Default frame with ORDER BY is RANGE to current row, so last_value needs an explicit frame and running totals need a unique tie-breaker. dense_rank plus QUALIFY handles tied top-N, max_by with a limit handles top-N arrays, grouping() labels subtotals, ON versus WHERE protects outer joins, and mergeable sketches and approx_percentile accuracy handle scale.

days.title: VARIANT for Semi-Structured Data and AI Functions such as ai_query in Pipelines

concepts.heading: Querying VARIANT: Paths, Case and Special Characters
concepts.body: Databricks recommends VARIANT over JSON strings for semi-structured data. Query syntax looks similar, with col:field, dot notation, brackets and a cast such as ::int, but several semantics differ and can break queries after a migration. All VARIANT path elements are matched case-sensitively, while JSON string queries are case-insensitive, so payload:Customer_ID returns NULL when the stored key is customer_id. The [*] syntax is not supported, and VARIANT encodes NULL differently. The dot operator selects a sub-field, so a key that contains a period, colon, space or bracket must be escaped: raw:['zip.code'] reads the field named zip.code, while raw:zip.code means field zip then sub-field code. To turn an array into rows, use a lateral variant_explode, which returns pos, key and value; for an array key is NULL and value is one element, still a VARIANT, so cast it: SELECT o.id, i.value:sku::string, i.value:qty::int FROM orders o, LATERAL variant_explode(o.payload:items) i. Input that is NULL or not an array or object yields no rows. Because the inner structure is not declared, schema_of_variant_agg(col) merges the schemas of all rows, including fields found in only some rows, to guide promoting stable fields into typed silver columns.

concepts.heading: Parsing, Nulls, Round Trips and Table Compatibility
concepts.body: parse_json raises an error on malformed input, so one truncated body fails the whole batch. try_parse_json returns NULL instead. The pattern is to parse with try_parse_json, send rows with a NULL result but non-NULL input to a rejects table, and let good rows flow. VARIANT also distinguishes two kinds of null. A missing path returns SQL NULL, so v:coupon IS NULL is true. A key that exists with an explicit JSON null returns a VARIANT holding null, for which IS NULL is false and is_variant_null is true. A data quality check that counts both cases separately uses both predicates. Parsing is not exactly reversible: to_json(variant) does not preserve whitespace, key order is arbitrary and trailing zeros in numbers may be truncated, so keep the raw STRING when you must prove the exact received text. For Delta tables, a table created with a VARIANT column has the feature enabled, and an existing table uses the table property delta.feature.variantType set to supported. Enabling it upgrades the writer protocol, which can break external Delta clients that do not support it.

concepts.heading: ai_query in Batch Pipelines: Scale, Errors and Structure
concepts.body: AI Functions are built for set-based, large-scale use from SQL, notebooks, Lakeflow pipelines and jobs. They manage parallelization, retries and scaling, so Databricks advises submitting the full dataset in one query instead of manually splitting it into slices in a Python loop. With ai_query, use Databricks-hosted foundation model endpoints for batch work. By default failOnError is true, so one endpoint error on a row fails the entire query and discards the work. With failOnError set to false each result becomes a STRUCT with the parsed response and an errorMessage, the response is NULL on failure, and failed rows can be selected and retried later. Chat models given only a prompt may wrap JSON in prose, which breaks a downstream from_json on a few percent of rows. The responseFormat argument, for chat foundation models, enforces the output shape with a DDL string such as STRUCT of vendor, total and due_date, or a JSON schema. The modelParameters struct, for settings such as max_tokens and temperature, must hold constant values, not data-dependent ones, so a per-row limit taken from a column is rejected; run separate queries per limit.

concepts.heading: Task-Specific Versus General Functions, Governance, Cost and Images
concepts.body: AI Functions come in two kinds. Task-specific functions such as ai_translate, ai_summarize or ai_classify cover one task with Databricks-managed approaches and no customization, and Databricks recommends them for getting started. ai_query is the general-purpose function for custom prompts and chosen models. Governance differs by kind. Where AI Functions Unity Catalog permissions are enabled, EXECUTE on the system.ai schema controls the task-specific functions: by default everyone has it, and an admin can remove it and grant EXECUTE on approved functions as an allow-list. That does not govern ai_query, which calls a Model Serving endpoint, so endpoint permissions control it. For cost, the compute running the query is always billed, and ai_query is billed for the endpoint you specify. Inference on Databricks-hosted endpoints is recorded in system.billing.usage with product MODEL_SERVING and offering type BATCH_INFERENCE, which includes ai_query workloads and can be joined to job metadata to rank jobs by LLM spend. For images, read files with read_files as binaryFile and pass files => content to a vision model; supported image inputs are JPEG and PNG, so convert other formats such as TIFF first.

examPoints: A question where a VARIANT query returns NULL after a migration from JSON strings is testing case-sensitive paths, and a key with a period is testing bracket escaping such as raw:['zip.code'].

A question about malformed JSON failing a nightly job is testing try_parse_json plus a rejects table, and one about proving exact received text is testing keeping the raw string because parse_json is not exactly reversible.

A question about errors in a large ai_query run is testing failOnError set to false, one about unreliable JSON output is testing responseFormat, and one about governance is testing that ai_query is controlled by endpoint permissions.

quiz.q: A batch job runs SELECT id, ai_query('databricks-llama', 'Summarize: ' || text) FROM tickets over 8 million rows. A few hundred rows hit endpoint errors and the whole query fails, discarding hours of work. The team wants the other rows to complete. What should they do?
choices: Add failOnError => false, so each result is a struct and failed rows can be retried
Wrap the call in a Python loop over 5,000-row slices so a failing slice is skipped on its own
Set modelParameters with a smaller max_tokens for each row so the endpoint stops returning errors
Switch to a task-specific function, which cannot fail because it ignores endpoint errors on each row
quiz.explain: failOnError false returns a struct with the response and an error message, so failures are isolated per row and retried later. Manual slicing fights the built-in parallelism and retries, and per-row model parameters must be constants.

quiz.q: A governance team removed EXECUTE on the system.ai schema from all users and granted it back for only ai_translate and ai_summarize. Analysts can still run ai_query against a hosted foundation model. Why?
choices: The EXECUTE grant on system.ai is cached for a day, so ai_query keeps working until the cache expires
Those grants do not govern ai_query, which calls a serving endpoint with its own permissions
Metastore admins automatically hold EXECUTE on every function, and the analysts share that role
ai_query is a task-specific function and therefore inherits EXECUTE from the other two granted functions
quiz.explain: The system.ai allow-list applies to the task-specific functions. ai_query calls a Model Serving endpoint, so access is controlled by permissions on that endpoint.

days.recap: VARIANT paths are case-sensitive, escape special characters with brackets, flatten arrays with variant_explode, parse tolerantly with try_parse_json, keep raw text for proof and mind the writer protocol upgrade. ai_query runs in one set-based query, uses failOnError false for isolation, responseFormat for structure, constant modelParameters, endpoint permissions for governance and MODEL_SERVING BATCH_INFERENCE for cost.

days.title: Data Quality Expectations in Lakeflow Pipelines: Actions, Quarantine, Failures and Metrics

concepts.heading: Three Actions and How to Choose Them
concepts.body: An expectation is a SQL boolean constraint evaluated on each record of a flow. Expectations apply to streaming tables, materialized views and views, and have three actions. Warn, the default expect, keeps invalid rows and records pass and fail counts. Drop, expect_or_drop, removes invalid rows from the target and logs how many were dropped, but the rows themselves are gone. Fail, expect_or_fail, stops the update when invalid records are unacceptable.
