A good rollout for a new source is to start with plain expect to measure how bad the data is, then switch the stable rules to expect_or_drop, and reserve fail for cases such as a broken primary key where continuing is worse than stopping. In SQL every expectation is its own named clause: CONSTRAINT valid_amount EXPECT (amount > 0) ON VIOLATION DROP ROW, where leaving out ON VIOLATION means warn and the other action is FAIL UPDATE. Python adds grouped decorators expect_all, expect_all_or_drop and expect_all_or_fail that take a dictionary, which has no SQL equivalent, so SQL authors repeat the clause per rule.

concepts.heading: Quarantine and Portable Rules
concepts.body: None of the three actions stores invalid rows separately, yet compliance often requires keeping them with a reason. The documented quarantine pattern keeps every row in one table with a boolean flag (the example makes it a temporary table, so persist a copy if review must outlive the update). You build a rule set and a quarantine condition, NOT(rule1 AND rule2), then add an is_quarantined column in a table that uses expect_all so metrics are still recorded. One view with is_quarantined false feeds the gold layer, and another view with true feeds the review process. Bad data stays available without polluting downstream tables. When the same eight rules apply to 25 datasets and change monthly, Databricks recommends storing expectation definitions separately from pipeline logic. A rules Delta table with name, constraint and tag columns, plus a helper such as get_rules(tag) that returns a dictionary, is passed to a decorator such as expect_all_or_drop. Tags group the rules, reuse is consistent across pipelines, and changes are audited as table changes without editing code. This portable pattern is a Python technique because the grouped decorators are Python only.

concepts.heading: What a Failed Expectation Does
concepts.body: Expectations enforce quality inside a flow; they are not orchestration. In a triggered pipeline a failed fail-expectation fails and rolls back only that flow's update, and other parallel flows continue independently, so a validation materialized view with expect_or_fail does not stop a downstream table from refreshing. In a continuous pipeline the failure stops the flow and all dependent flows, and the pipeline emits a message with the reason. The update is rolled back atomically and manual intervention is needed: fix the pipeline code so it handles the invalid data, then restart. For real gating, split validation and downstream work into separate pipelines and coordinate them with control flow between the pipeline tasks in Lakeflow Jobs. To find the offending record, remember that fail expectations modify the query plan so the violating record can be tracked. The update fails with an EXPECTATION_VIOLATION message naming the violated expectations and including the input data and the output record, which works for many queries but not all. Fail actions record no pass and fail metrics.

concepts.heading: Metrics, the Event Log and Limits
concepts.body: Metrics for warn and drop actions are recorded in flow_progress events of the pipeline event log, and the Data quality tab shows them too. For some flows a COMPLETED event does not contain the metrics, because they are reported per micro-batch in flow_progress events with status RUNNING, so a sum over COMPLETED rows alone misses counts. Streaming tables and materialized views created in Databricks SQL are backed by a standalone pipeline. They support CONSTRAINT expectations, but the Data quality tab of the pipeline UI is not available for them, so query the event log instead. Metrics are also absent when no expectations are defined, when an update had no new data, or when the operator or flow type does not support expectations, for example some sinks. Expectations are not supported with AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT: a constraint on that target gives neither enforcement nor metrics, so put the check on a downstream dataset that reads the dimension. Constraints must be valid SQL conditions, evaluated per record to true or false.

examPoints: A question that must keep bad rows for review but keep them out of gold is testing the quarantine pattern with an is_quarantined flag and two views, because drop, warn and fail do not store invalid rows separately.
A question where a downstream table still updated after expect_or_fail is testing that a triggered pipeline rolls back only the failing flow, while a continuous pipeline stops dependent flows too.

A question about missing metrics is testing flow_progress events with status RUNNING, the missing Data quality tab for standalone SQL pipelines, or the lack of expectation support in AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT.

quiz.q: A streaming table receives trip records. Rows with a NULL pickup or dropoff zip must not reach gold reports, but compliance requires keeping them for review with the reason. Which design in a Lakeflow pipeline meets both needs?
choices: Use expect_or_drop on both columns and read the dropped rows from the pipeline event log later
Use expect_or_fail so the pipeline stops, then repair the rows by hand before restarting
Flag rows as is_quarantined using expect_all, then expose valid and invalid rows as two views
Use plain expect and filter the invalid rows in every downstream query with its own WHERE clause
quiz.explain: The documented quarantine pattern keeps all rows with a flag so valid rows feed gold and invalid rows feed review. The event log holds counts and not the dropped rows, and fail stops everything.

quiz.q: A triggered pipeline has a validation materialized view with expect_or_fail on a primary key check. The check fails, yet a downstream table in the same pipeline still refreshed. The team expected it to be blocked. What explains this?
choices: The expectation was evaluated at the end of the update, after downstream tables had already committed
The pipeline was set to development mode, in which expectation failures never stop other flows
Fail expectations act only in continuous pipelines, so in a triggered one the action silently becomes warn
Only the failing flow is rolled back in a triggered pipeline; validation tables do not gate others
quiz.explain: In a triggered pipeline a failed expectation rolls back only that flow, and other flows continue independently. Gating needs separate pipelines coordinated with control flow.

days.recap: Warn measures, drop removes, fail stops. Quarantine with a flag when bad rows must be kept, portable rules tables and expect_all decorators in Python, one named CONSTRAINT per rule in SQL. Triggered pipelines roll back only the failing flow, continuous ones stop dependents. Read metrics from flow_progress including RUNNING events, and put checks after AUTO CDC FROM SNAPSHOT.

days.title: System Tables for Cost, Audit and Workload Monitoring

concepts.heading: Billing Usage and Correction Records
concepts.body: `system.billing.usage` holds one row per billable usage period, with the SKU, the quantity, `usage_metadata` (which job, cluster, warehouse or pipeline caused it) and `custom_tags`. The billing tables are global: a workspace in any region shows the whole account. Databricks also corrects past records. When a record was wrong, it adds two new rows instead of editing the old one: a `RETRACTION` with an identical row but a negative `usage_quantity` that cancels the original, and a `RESTATEMENT` with the corrected values. Only the `ORIGINAL` rows are the normal case, so a filter such as `record_type = 'ORIGINAL'` looks tidy but keeps the wrong numbers for any corrected month. Sum every row instead: the retraction cancels the original and the restatement supplies the right amount. A correction can also consist of a retraction alone when the usage should never have been recorded. To turn quantity into money, join `system.billing.list_prices` on the SKU and the price validity window; the price table is a history, so one SKU has several rows over time.

concepts.heading: Attributing Cost to Jobs, Clusters and Pipelines
concepts.body: Attribution depends on what the compute was. `usage_metadata.job_id` is filled for serverless jobs and for jobs on job compute, but not for a job that runs on all-purpose compute. That usage is billed under the ALL_PURPOSE product and carries only `cluster_id`, so a dashboard that groups by `job_id` shows the cost vanishing when a job is moved to a shared cluster. For such cases attribute through `cluster_id` and join the cluster's tags or owner from `system.compute.clusters`. Pipelines carry their own identifier in `usage_metadata`, and `billing_origin_product` separates products such as jobs, pipelines and SQL. The most reliable lever for chargeback is tagging: `custom_tags` set on compute appear on the usage rows, so cost can be grouped by team without joins. Moving recurring jobs from all-purpose clusters to job compute is both cheaper and gives job-level billing records, which is why platform teams look for jobs whose tasks still run on interactive clusters.

concepts.heading: Lakeflow Tables: SCD2, Regional Scope and Run History
concepts.body: The `system.lakeflow` schema describes jobs and pipelines. `jobs`, `job_tasks` and `pipelines` are slowly changing dimension tables: every rename or schedule edit adds a row, and a delete adds a row with `delete_time` set. Joining usage to them directly multiplies the cost for every edited job. Reduce the table to its latest row per entity first (a window over `change_time` descending, `ROW_NUMBER() = 1`), then drop deleted entities, and only then join. The run tables `job_run_timeline`, `job_task_run_timeline` and `pipeline_update_timeline` are immutable and need no deduplication; the task timeline reports durations per task run and lists the compute in `compute_ids`. Unlike billing, these tables are regional: they contain the workspaces of the same cloud region only, so a name lookup for an eu job must run from an eu workspace even though its usage is visible everywhere. Free retention is limited to about a year, except that the newest row of every SCD2 entity is always kept.

concepts.heading: Compute, Lineage and Access to System Tables
concepts.body: `system.compute.node_timeline` stores utilization per node per minute with a flag for the driver, so a team can see that a driver (for example after large collects) was saturated while workers idled, even after the cluster has terminated. `system.compute.clusters` keeps configuration history, including `cluster_source`. The lineage tables `table_lineage` and `column_lineage` are a subset of all reads and writes: records appear only when lineage can be inferred, so an empty result is weak evidence that a table is unused and a staged deprecation is the safe route. Access is governed by Unity Catalog. By default only users who are both account admin and metastore admin can read system tables, and the tables are read-only. To share them, grant `USE CATALOG` on `system`, `USE SCHEMA` and `SELECT` on the schemas. To give a team lead only the lead's own workspaces, grant `SELECT` on a view in a governed schema that filters the usage rows. The audit log table is still in Public Preview, so exam answers rest on the other tables.

examPoints: Corrections arrive as RETRACTION plus RESTATEMENT rows: sum all record types, never filter to ORIGINAL.
job_id is empty for jobs on all-purpose compute; attribute through cluster_id and cluster tags. jobs, job_tasks and pipelines are SCD2: take the latest row first.
Billing is global but lakeflow tables are regional; share system tables through a filtered view, not broad grants.

quiz.q: A finance report totals usage_quantity from system.billing.usage with WHERE record_type = 'ORIGINAL' to avoid negative values. For a month with corrections the total no longer matches the invoice. What should the engineer change?
choices: Keep the filter and add RESTATEMENT rows only, because a retraction cancels the corrected amount a second time
Remove the filter and sum every row, so each retraction cancels its original and the restatement adds the corrected amount
Join system.billing.list_prices first and drop every row whose price is missing, because corrections never carry a SKU price
Filter on usage_end_time of the previous month only, because corrected usage is always written into the month that follows
quiz.explain: The original, the retraction (negative quantity, otherwise identical) and the restatement together net to the corrected amount. Filtering to ORIGINAL keeps the wrong figure; keeping only restatements ignores uncorrected usage. Price joins and end-time windows do not govern corrections.

quiz.q: A report joins system.billing.usage to system.lakeflow.jobs on workspace and job ID and shows totals above the billed amount for jobs that were renamed or rescheduled. What is the fix?
choices: Add DISTINCT to the select list, because the jobs table repeats the same job once for every workspace in the whole region
Read the report from a workspace in another region, because the jobs table duplicates its rows across regions to survive regional outages
Reduce jobs to the latest row per workspace and job by change_time, exclude deleted jobs, and then join usage to that result
Replace the join with job_run_timeline, because the jobs table is only filled for jobs that never changed their definition
quiz.explain: jobs is an SCD2 table: each edit adds a row, so a plain join multiplies usage by the number of versions. Taking the newest row per entity first fixes it. DISTINCT does not undo multiplied sums, and regions do not duplicate rows.

days.recap: Billing is global, additive and corrected through retraction and restatement rows; lakeflow history is regional and SCD2, so reduce to the latest row before joining. Know which compute fills job_id, and expose system tables through views.

days.title: Monitoring with REST, CLI, SDK and Pipeline Event Logs

concepts.heading: Reading Runs Through the Jobs API
concepts.body: `runs/list` answers questions such as how many runs failed last night, but it is paged. The `limit` parameter allows at most 25 runs per page (default 20), and the response carries `next_page_token`, which you pass back as `page_token`. A script that reads one page undercounts as the run volume grows, which is a classic cause of counts that stop matching the Jobs UI. `completed_only` and `active_only` are mutually exclusive filters, and `expand_tasks=true` returns task details inside each run. Arrays inside a run are paged too: a single run returns the first 100 elements of `tasks`, `job_clusters`, `job_parameters` and `repair_history`, and `runs/get` returns a `next_page_token` for more. A run that shows Succeeded may have been repaired after an earlier failure; `runs/get` with `include_history=true` (or `--include-history` in the CLI) adds the `repair_history` so on-call can see which repairs happened and when. The CLI mirrors the REST endpoints, so the same pagination rules apply to scripts built on it.

concepts.heading: Task Output, SDK and Authentication
concepts.body: A multi-task job run has one run ID for the job and a separate `run_id` for every task inside `tasks`. `runs/get-output` works on a task run: the value a notebook returns through `dbutils.notebook.exit()` is retrieved by passing the task's `run_id`, taken from `get-run`, and not the job run ID returned by `run-now`. The API returns at most the first 5 MB of output, so larger results should be written to cloud storage. The Databricks SDK for Python implements unified authentication: `WorkspaceClient()` with no arguments discovers credentials from the environment, and the same configuration works for the CLI and other SDKs. For unattended monitors, use a service principal with OAuth machine-to-machine credentials rather than a personal token. Create one client and reuse it, fanning out with a thread pool when many objects need polling. The pipelines events endpoint has a similar paging rule: a call with `page_token` may carry only `max_results` besides it, because the token already encodes the filter.

concepts.heading: Where the Pipeline Event Log Lives and Who Can Read It
concepts.body: Every pipeline writes an event log: a record of user actions, update and flow lifecycle, data quality and resource events. By default it is a hidden Delta table named `event_log_<pipeline id>` in the pipeline's default catalog and schema. It is not shown in Catalog Explorer; you read it with the `event_log(<pipeline id>)` table-valued function, and by default only the run-as user of the pipeline may query it. To let an SRE team read it without exposing more, publish the log in the pipeline settings under a name and, optionally, a catalog and schema. Then create a view over the published table and grant `SELECT` on the view, not on the table itself, because the event log location also serves as the schema location for Auto Loader in the pipeline. Views over event logs support streaming queries. Never delete the event log or its parent catalog or schema: the pipeline can fail on later updates. The Jobs-and-pipelines UI, the Pipelines REST API and the log all show the same events.

concepts.heading: What the Event Log Tells You
concepts.body: Pick the event type for the question. `update_progress` describes the lifecycle of an update, so the final state and duration of each update come from the latest such event per `origin.update_id`. `flow_progress` covers the lifecycle of a flow and carries metrics, including `backlog_bytes` and `source_metrics` for sources such as Auto Loader or Kafka, which give an early warning that a running update is falling behind. `planning_information` explains why a materialized view or REPLACE WHERE flow is fully recomputed instead of incrementally refreshed. `operation_progress` events of type `AUTO_LOADER_LISTING` carry `duration_ms` and show when directory listing slows an update before data is processed. `cluster_resources` and `autoscale` events exist only for classic compute, so a serverless pipeline produces none. Data quality sits under `flow_progress`: `dropped_records` counts each dropped row once, while the `expectations` array has `passed_records` and `failed_records` per rule. A row that breaks three rules adds one to each rule, so per-rule failures must not be summed to get the number of bad records.

examPoints: runs/list pages hold at most 25 runs: follow next_page_token with page_token; runs/get with include_history shows repairs.
get-run-output needs the task run_id from get-run, not the job run ID; pipeline event pages after the first take only page_token plus max_results.
Publish the event log, expose a view, grant SELECT on the view. update_progress for update state, flow_progress for backlog and quality, planning_information for MV recompute.

quiz.q: A nightly script calls runs/list with completed_only=true and counts failed runs. As the daily run count grew, the totals stopped matching the Jobs UI although the filter did not change. What is the cause and the fix?
choices: The call returns one page of at most 25 runs, so the script has to follow next_page_token with page_token until none is returned
The completed_only filter hides runs that were repaired, so the script has to call runs/get with include_history for every run it counts
The response truncates the run list at the time window, so the script has to widen start_time_from by one day for every missing run
The endpoint samples runs when a job has many, so the script has to raise the limit to the maximum and call again for the remainder
quiz.explain: runs/list is paginated; each response has at most 25 runs and a next_page_token. Without following it the script sees only the first page. It is not sampling, and repairs are a separate matter.

quiz.q: A materialized view in a pipeline is expected to refresh incrementally, but a refresh after a code change took as long as a full recompute. Which event log information shows how the refresh was planned?
choices: flow_progress events, whose data quality section lists the techniques that the refresh considered and the techniques that it finally rejected
autoscale events, which record the cluster resize requests that forced the planner to choose a complete recompute of the view
update_progress events, whose details state the refresh technique and the reason that an earlier technique was not selected
planning_information events, which list the candidate refresh techniques, the chosen one and any issues that prevented it
quiz.explain: planning_information explains why a materialized view was fully recomputed, including incrementalization issues. flow_progress carries metrics and quality counters, update_progress tracks update state, and autoscale events are only for classic compute resizing.

days.recap: Page every list call, use task run IDs for output, and read pipeline state from the event log through a published view. Match the event type to the question: update_progress, flow_progress, planning_information, operation_progress.

days.title: Alerts and Monitoring Runs in the Jobs UI and API

concepts.heading: How an Alert Evaluates
concepts.body: A Databricks SQL alert runs its own query on a schedule against a SQL warehouse and compares one value with a threshold. An evaluation ends as `OK`, `TRIGGERED` or `ERROR`; the older `UNKNOWN` state does not exist in the latest alerts, and each alert owns its query instead of reusing a saved one. The value can come from the first row of a column or from an aggregation across all rows. That choice matters: a query that returns one row per region with the condition on the first value only watches whichever region sorts first, so a drop in another region goes unnoticed. Either make the query return a single summarizing row or select MIN, MAX or SUM in the condition. Advanced settings add Notify on OK for recovery messages, a notification template, and the Empty result state. A freshness check such as `SELECT max(load_time) ... WHERE load_date = current_date()` returns no rows when the load never ran. The Empty result state setting chooses which state (OK, TRIGGERED or ERROR) such an empty result reports, so setting it to TRIGGERED turns a missing load into a signal.

concepts.heading: Scheduling, Jobs Integration and Git Folders
concepts.body: A workspace limits how many alert runs can be active at once. When all slots are taken at the moment a schedule fires, that run is skipped and the alert does not evaluate; the evaluation history shows a gap with no error. The typical pattern is dozens of alerts sharing one cron time, while a manual Run now works because it runs outside the spike. The fix is to stagger schedules by a few minutes. An alert can also be a task in a job, so downstream tasks can branch on it. That SQL alert task reports Succeeded whenever the alert was evaluated, whether the condition was triggered or not, and Failed only if the evaluation itself errors, so a triggered alert does not fail the run or fire the job's failure notification by itself. It needs a serverless or pro warehouse. Alerts can be tracked in Databricks Git folders, but newly cloned alerts appear in the list only after a user interacts with them, and their schedules are paused until someone resumes each one. After a first release to production, silence usually means paused schedules, not broken queries.

concepts.heading: Monitoring Runs in the Jobs UI
concepts.body: The Runs tab keeps history for 60 days for jobs and pipelines. If auditors need the rendered output of every run for longer, export the notebook run results before they expire and store the files elsewhere, because expired runs and their outputs are not kept. The matrix view shows a history of runs with one bar per run and per task, where the bar height shows duration and the colors show status, so a task that slowly grows over 30 runs is visible without any query. With an expected completion time configured, the matrix warns when a run exceeds it. A `For each` task presents its iterations as a table instead of one cell, and the Only failed iterations toggle reduces 400 iterations to the ones that failed, each opening its own output. Runs sent to `runs/submit`, including those from the Airflow `DatabricksSubmitRunOperator`, are one-time runs without a saved job, so searching by job name finds nothing; filter by Run ID, Run as or Start time, or create a job to get durable, searchable runs.

concepts.heading: Monitoring at Scale with SQL
concepts.body: The UI is for one job; fleets are monitored with SQL. `system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline` and `job_task_run_timeline` give run and task durations and results, so a query can rank tasks by growing duration or count failures per week. The task timeline lists `compute_ids`; joining them to the latest row of `system.compute.clusters` and keeping `cluster_source` values `UI` or `API` finds tasks that run on interactive clusters and should move to job compute. For alerts themselves, `system.alert.alerts` is a slowly changing table of every alert's configuration, and `system.alert.alert_evaluation_history` has one row per evaluation with its evaluated state and error details. A weekly query over evaluations that ended in `ERROR`, or a count of schedules with gaps, finds monitors that are silently broken. These tables are regional, retain data for 395 days for alerts and about a year for lakeflow, and arrive typically within an hour. Combine them with a Databricks SQL alert on top: monitoring the monitors.

examPoints: Alert conditions read the first row or an aggregation: use MIN/MAX/SUM or a single-row query. Set Empty result state to TRIGGERED when no rows means failure.
Skipped scheduled alert runs come from the active-run limit: stagger schedules. A SQL alert task succeeds whenever evaluation succeeds, triggered or not.
Run history lasts 60 days (export to keep); For each has an Only failed iterations toggle; runs/submit runs have no job name.

quiz.q: An alert query returns one row per region with pct_change, ordered by region name. The condition uses the first value of pct_change below -20. Revenue falls 35% in a region that is not first, and no alert fires. What should the engineer do?
choices: Use an aggregation such as MIN on pct_change in the condition, or return one summarizing row
Set the Empty result state to TRIGGERED, because a region that is not listed first is treated as a missing result by the alert evaluation
Enable Notify on OK, because without a recovery message the alert suppresses every further trigger after its first evaluation
Schedule the alert at a lower frequency, because rows beyond the first are only evaluated when the schedule is stretched out
quiz.explain: The condition looks at the first value only, so other rows are invisible. An aggregation over all rows, or a single-row result, makes every region count. Empty result handling and recovery notifications address different situations.

quiz.q: A job runs a SQL alert task. One morning the alert condition was met, but the task shows Succeeded and the job's failure notification did not fire. How should the engineer interpret this?
choices: The warehouse hit its timeout, because a triggered alert reports success only when the notification destination did not answer
It works as designed: the task succeeds once the alert was evaluated, triggered or not, and fails only if the evaluation errors
The task was skipped by the run-if setting of the job, because alert tasks only report triggered alerts as failures after a full retry cycle
The alert schedule overrode the task, because the job run evaluates the alert on its own cron expression and ignores the result
quiz.explain: The SQL alert task status describes whether the evaluation worked, not whether the condition was met. A triggered alert still means a Succeeded task; downstream tasks or the alert's own subscribers handle the signal.

days.recap: Alerts need a condition that sees every row, an explicit empty-result state, and staggered schedules. The Jobs UI keeps 60 days of runs; fleets are watched with lakeflow and alert system tables.

days.title: Managed Tables, Predictive Optimization and Delta Layout Choices

concepts.heading: Managed Tables and Predictive Optimization
concepts.body: Unity Catalog managed tables are the foundation of low-maintenance Delta: Databricks manages the storage location and the table lifecycle. Dropping a managed table deletes its files after a recovery period (7 days by default), while the files of an external table stay in storage until you delete them yourself. Predictive optimization runs `OPTIMIZE`, `VACUUM` and `ANALYZE` on managed tables for you. It can be enabled at account, catalog, schema or table level with inheritance, and the work runs on serverless compute for jobs, so no team cluster is sized for it and the account is billed through a serverless jobs SKU. Two details matter for design. First, `OPTIMIZE` run by predictive optimization does not apply `ZORDER`, and it ignores Z-ordered files, so a nightly Z-order job cannot simply be retired. The path forward is liquid clustering, which it does maintain. Second, its `VACUUM` honors `delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration` (default 7 days): set 30 days before enabling it if time travel of that length is needed.

concepts.heading: Liquid Clustering and Where Its Overhead Goes
concepts.body: Liquid clustering replaces partitioning and `ZORDER`; it cannot be combined with either. You declare `CLUSTER BY (col, ...)` with up to four keys, and data is organized incrementally by `OPTIMIZE`, so changing keys does not rewrite the table. The maintenance burden disappears only if the work runs. Clustering on write happens when a transaction reaches a size threshold, which is lower for managed tables, so a stream appending 5 MB micro-batches leaves new data mostly unclustered and data skipping degrades over weeks. Predictive optimization closes the gap by running incremental clustering in the background. Streaming writes can be clustered on write with `spark.databricks.delta.liquid.eagerClustering.streaming.enabled`, but the size condition still applies. Clustering keys must have statistics: by default only the first 32 columns are covered, so on an external table a key in column 70 of a wide table does not skip files until you add it with `delta.dataSkippingStatsColumns` and recompute with `ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE DELTA STATISTICS`. On managed tables, predictive optimization also collects statistics on frequently filtered columns beyond the first 32.

concepts.heading: Choosing a Technique by Access Pattern
concepts.body: Match the technique to the bottleneck. A nightly `MERGE` that touches 0.1% of the rows but scattered over most files is a write problem: without deletion vectors each touched file is rewritten. With deletion vectors changed rows are marked in metadata, reads apply the marks, and files are physically rewritten later, for example by `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)` or auto-compaction. Selective dashboard filters are a read problem and call for clustering keys. A table with both patterns uses both, because they address different costs. Deletion vectors upgrade the table protocol, so a client without support fails on reads; in newer runtimes you can drop the feature to restore compatibility. They also do not guarantee that files are physically rewritten soon: compaction may skip files, so `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)` forces the rewrite and `VACUUM` then removes the old files. A stable access pattern on external storage can use manual keys, and Z-order on columns without statistics only wastes compute.

concepts.heading: Automatic Clustering and Choosing Keys
concepts.body: `CLUSTER BY AUTO` lets Databricks choose and change keys from the table's query history. It is available only for Unity Catalog managed tables and depends on predictive optimization, which runs the selection asynchronously. It is cost-aware: keys change only when the predicted saving from data skipping outweighs the clustering cost, and it may pick none for tables that are too small or already well ordered. To start from a hint and still adapt, set manual keys first and then enable automatic mode: `ALTER TABLE sales CLUSTER BY (region); ALTER TABLE sales CLUSTER BY AUTO;`. A trap: running `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE` on an automatic table without `CLUSTER BY AUTO` turns the mode off and drops the chosen columns, so restate the clause. When keys differ strongly in cardinality, hierarchical clustering through `delta.liquid.hierarchicalClusteringColumns` prioritizes a low-cardinality column such as `event_date`; keep high-cardinality columns such as `device_id` as standard keys. Manual hierarchical settings are respected by predictive optimization.

examPoints: Predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE (never ZORDER), VACUUM and ANALYZE on managed tables, on serverless jobs compute; set deletedFileRetentionDuration before relying on its VACUUM.
Deletion vectors fix write cost of scattered MERGE; clustering fixes read skipping; they combine. DVs upgrade the protocol; REORG PURGE forces the physical rewrite, then VACUUM.

CLUSTER BY AUTO: managed tables only; CREATE OR REPLACE without it turns it off; clustering keys need statistics (first 32 columns on external tables; managed tables gain more through predictive optimization).

quiz.q: A team replaced a nightly OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (customer_id) job with predictive optimization. Weeks later, customer_id filters scan more files than before. What explains this and what is the right change?
choices: Predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE without ZORDER; move the table to liquid clustering on customer_id
Predictive optimization runs VACUUM before OPTIMIZE, so Z-ordered files are removed too early; shorten the retention window to repair the layout
Predictive optimization only starts after 30 days on a table, so the Z-order simply has to wait until the first scheduled run completes
Predictive optimization removes statistics on Z-ordered columns, so the table has to be partitioned by customer_id to regain skipping
quiz.explain: OPTIMIZE run by predictive optimization does not apply ZORDER and ignores Z-ordered files. Liquid clustering is the layout it maintains. There is no 30-day delay, and VACUUM does not reorder files.

quiz.q: Streaming micro-batches of about 5 MB are appended to a liquid-clustered managed table. Data skipping on the clustering keys gets worse over weeks and predictive optimization is turned off. What is the most likely reason and the remedy?
choices: Clustering keys can be changed only with append mode, so the streaming writer silently resets them; use overwrite for every micro-batch
Statistics are collected only for the first 32 columns of the stream schema, so every new key has to be repeated in the stream checkpoint
Small transactions stay below the clustering-on-write threshold; enable predictive optimization so incremental clustering runs
Liquid clustering is rebuilt once per day by VACUUM, so the layout only looks worse until the next scheduled vacuum has finished
quiz.explain: Clustering on write triggers only when a transaction reaches a size threshold, so small batches stay unclustered. Running OPTIMIZE or enabling predictive optimization clusters them incrementally. VACUUM does not cluster data.

days.recap: Managed tables plus predictive optimization remove most maintenance, but it never runs ZORDER and its VACUUM follows the retention property. Choose deletion vectors for write cost, clustering for read skipping, and CLUSTER BY AUTO for changing patterns on managed tables.

days.title: Caching for Repeated Reads and Change Data Feed

concepts.heading: The Disk Cache
concepts.body: When a node reads a Parquet file from cloud storage, Databricks copies it to the node's local storage in a fast format, and later reads of the same data run locally. This disk cache serves all Parquet files, including Delta tables, needs no code changes, and is enabled automatically on worker types that support it. The easiest setup is a cache-accelerated worker type with local SSD. The cache uses at most half of the local SSD space by default. It detects created, deleted, modified and overwritten files and evicts stale entries by itself, so after a `MERGE` or `OPTIMIZE` nobody has to invalidate anything, and jobs that try are unnecessary. On SQL warehouses and recent runtimes `CACHE SELECT` is ignored because an enhanced disk caching algorithm is used instead, so a manual warm-up step does nothing. To measure cold reads for a benchmark, set `spark.databricks.io.cache.enabled` to `false`: queries then neither read from nor add to the cache, and nothing needs to be deleted.

concepts.heading: Disk Cache versus Spark Cache
concepts.body: The two caches solve different problems. The disk cache stores copies of source files on local disk; it makes repeated scans of the same files cheap but stores no transformation results. The Apache Spark cache, created with `df.cache()` or `persist`, stores a DataFrame's computed partitions in memory and on disk. If a heavy join and aggregation result feeds five actions, persisting that DataFrame avoids repeating the join, which the disk cache cannot do. The Spark cache has a weakness on elastic clusters: when a worker is decommissioned by autoscaling, the cached blocks on it are lost and Spark rereads or recomputes the missing partitions, so the second report can be slower than the first although the data is unchanged. Release it with `unpersist` when finished. The Databricks recommendation for repeated reads of Parquet and Delta data is the automatic disk cache; reserve the Spark cache for expensive intermediate results reused several times in one session. On serverless compute `df.cache()` behaves differently from the classic Spark cache.

concepts.heading: Change Data Feed for Incremental Downstream Processing
concepts.body: Change data feed exposes row-level changes between table versions: each change row carries the data plus `_change_type` (`insert`, `update_preimage`, `update_postimage`, `delete`), `_commit_version` and a timestamp. Two forms exist, both read with `table_changes()` or the `readChangeFeed` option. Legacy CDF is switched on with `delta.enableChangeDataFeed` and writes change data at write time, which costs write overhead and storage on heavy `MERGE` and `UPDATE` jobs. Automatic CDF computes changes at read time from row tracking (Delta) or row lineage (Iceberg v3), so it needs no per-table setting and adds no write cost; it needs managed or external Delta tables with row tracking on a recent runtime. You cannot use both: to migrate, unset the legacy property and keep the same read code. CDF is transient: the feed is removed with old versions and `VACUUM`, so it is not an audit trail. For a permanent history, run a `readChangeFeed` stream, for example with an `availableNow` trigger and its own checkpoint, that appends the changes to a separate history table.

concepts.heading: Reading the Feed Correctly
concepts.body: Several rows can describe one key. An update yields a `update_preimage` and a `update_postimage` row, and a key changed in several commits appears repeatedly in a version range. Feeding that raw range into a `MERGE` fails with a multiple-match error, because several source rows match one target row. A common pattern, not a documented rule, is to drop the preimage rows, keep the highest `_commit_version` per key, and apply deletes where `_change_type = 'delete'`. In Structured Streaming, Databricks tracks the version for you through the checkpoint; if the checkpoint is lost, start a new stream with a new checkpoint and `startingVersion` set to one more than the last version the target already reflects, not at zero. A batch hourly job that stores its own last version can fail on quiet hours because the start version is beyond the last commit; setting `spark.databricks.delta.changeDataFeed.timestampOutOfRange.enabled` makes it return an empty result. On tables with column mapping, a query cannot span a non-additive schema change such as a rename or drop: split the range into parts before and after it.

examPoints: Disk cache: automatic, SSD workers, evicts stale files by itself, ignores CACHE SELECT on warehouses. Spark cache stores results but is lost when autoscaling removes workers.
Automatic CDF (row tracking, no write overhead) replaces legacy delta.enableChangeDataFeed; both cannot be active together, and the read APIs stay the same.
CDF is transient: keep history in your own table. A common pattern is to dedupe preimage/postimage rows by key and latest _commit_version; restart a stream at last applied version + 1.

quiz.q: A notebook computes a heavy join and aggregation and then uses the resulting DataFrame in five actions. The cluster has SSD workers with the disk cache on, but the join still runs five times. What reduces the repeated work?
choices: Persist the joined DataFrame with the Spark cache, because the disk cache holds source file copies, not results
Run CACHE SELECT on the source tables first, because that command stores the join output in the disk cache on every single worker
Enable the disk cache at the notebook level, because the cluster setting does not apply to DataFrames that were created from joins
Switch the workers to network-attached storage, because local SSD copies of the files force every action to recompute the join
quiz.explain: The disk cache stores source file copies; it does not keep the result of a join. df.cache() or persist keeps the computed partitions for later actions. CACHE SELECT does not store transformation output.

quiz.q: A downstream job reads table_changes('customers', 41, 45) and merges every row into a dimension table. Several customers appear more than once with update_preimage and update_postimage rows, and the MERGE fails with a multiple-match error. What is the fix?
choices: Run the MERGE with delete semantics only, because preimage rows are the correct images of every customer in the range
Read each version on its own, because a range query is not supported once more than one commit touches the same customer
Disable row tracking on the table, because the duplicate rows come from automatic change data feed and not from the table itself
Drop update_preimage rows, keep the highest _commit_version row per customer_id, and apply deletes from _change_type = 'delete'
quiz.explain: A range can contain several changes per key plus preimage images. Keeping the newest postimage per key and applying deletes gives one source row per target row. Range reads are supported and the duplicates are normal in the feed.

days.recap: Rely on the automatic disk cache for repeated file reads and use persist only for reused results, remembering that autoscaling drops Spark cache blocks. Use change data feed for incremental processing, keep your own history, and deduplicate change rows per key.

days.title: Query Profile Bottlenecks and Liquid Clustering versus Partitioning

concepts.heading: Reading the Query Profile and Its Insights
concepts.body: The query profile shows the plan as a graph with per-operator metrics, and Databricks attaches performance insights ranked by their estimated effect on total task duration. Start from the insight, then confirm it in the operators. A query answered from the query cache has no profile; to capture one, make a trivial change such as changing or removing the `LIMIT`. `EXPLODING_JOIN` flags a join that outputs far more rows than it reads, for example 3 million orders against 50,000 customers producing 900 million rows: decide which result subset you need, then tighten the join condition or reduce the input rows; a non-unique key on the dimension side is a typical cause to check. `SELECTIVE_JOIN` suggests filtering before the join, `WIDE_PROJECTION` suggests selecting only needed columns, and `REDUNDANT_JOIN` and `REDUNDANT_AGGREGATION` point to work that did not change the result. `COVERAGE_FILTER_KEYS_CLUSTERING` and its partitioning twin mean filters do not use the table's layout keys, so adding filters on those keys reduces bytes read. Insights labelled Accelerated, such as `HISTORY_BASED_JOIN_STRATEGY`, describe optimizations Databricks already applied and need no action.

concepts.heading: Data Layout Insights
concepts.body: `COVERAGE_STATS_DELTA` says file-skipping statistics are missing or incomplete for the scan's filters, with a status of Full, Partial, Unavailable or Unused (the filter converts the data type). The remedy is to make the filtered column a statistics column with `delta.dataSkippingStatsColumns` and recompute with `ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE DELTA STATISTICS` so existing files get statistics. By default external tables collect statistics on the first 32 columns, so a filter on column 80 of a wide table scans nearly everything. `DATA_FILE_SIZE` reports many small files: enable predictive optimization or run `OPTIMIZE`, and for a partitioned table consider liquid clustering, because predictive optimization cannot compact small files across partitions. `DATA_SKEW` means uneven distribution, as when 70% of rows have a NULL key; the remedy is key salting or pre-aggregation in two stages, group by the key and a random salt first and then combine. `MANUAL_DATA_LAYOUT` recommends managed tables, predictive optimization and automatic clustering, and `CONCURRENT_WRITE` points to write conflicts: review the Delta history and adjust scheduling.

concepts.heading: Compute Insights and Plan Differences
concepts.body: `DATA_SPILL` means data did not fit in memory. The first recommendation is a larger warehouse; when size is fixed by policy, reduce what the operators carry: select only needed columns before the join and sort, so a 4 KB `raw_payload` string is not held in memory for every row. `EXCESSIVE_QUEUE_TIME` appears when a query's wall-clock time is mostly waiting for warehouse capacity, for example dozens of dashboards refreshing at 09:00; the recommendation is a higher maximum number of clusters, which adds capacity when queries queue, while execution time itself is fine. `IO_THROTTLING` points to cloud storage request limits and is a matter for administrators. Plans can legitimately differ between `EXPLAIN` and the profile. `EXPLAIN` does not run the query, so it shows the plan before adaptive query execution applies runtime statistics, for instance a sort merge join; the executed query can switch to a broadcast join when a side turns out small. Skip a `BROADCAST` hint when the optimizer already chose broadcast: Spark prioritizes a hinted broadcast even above `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold`, so the hint can stay in force as the table grows.

concepts.heading: Liquid Clustering versus Partitioning and ZORDER
concepts.body: Choose liquid clustering for new tables, especially with high-cardinality filters, skew, fast growth, concurrent writers or changing patterns; it is incompatible with partitioning and `ZORDER`. Telemetry filtered by `device_id` (millions of values) and a recent `event_date` range suits `CLUSTER BY (event_date, device_id)` with predictive optimization, not a partition on `device_id`. Keys accept struct fields in dot notation such as `device.model`. A table that was fast through natural ingestion order but degrades under scattered `UPDATE` and `MERGE` gains from clustering on a matching date column. Clustering also allows row-level concurrency, so concurrent `MERGE` jobs touching different rows of the same partition conflict far less. To convert a partitioned Delta table, use `ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY`, keep the new columns close to the old partition columns to avoid a large first `OPTIMIZE`, and run `OPTIMIZE`. Managed Iceberg tables already use partition definitions as clustering keys, so the command errors for them. For a pipeline streaming table, change `PARTITIONED BY` to `CLUSTER BY` in the source. Clustered Delta tables need writer version 7 and reader version 3, so older readers may need the old layout.

examPoints: Read the insight first: EXPLODING_JOIN (check key uniqueness), COVERAGE_STATS_DELTA (statistics columns + ANALYZE), DATA_SKEW (salt or pre-aggregate), EXCESSIVE_QUEUE_TIME (max clusters).
A cached query has no profile (change LIMIT). EXPLAIN shows the plan before execution; AQE adapts it at run time, so trust the profile.

Liquid clustering replaces partitioning and ZORDER; convert with REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY; managed Iceberg errors; pipeline tables change their definition; old readers keep the old layout.

quiz.q: A selective query on a wide external Delta table filters on tenant_id and scans nearly every file. Its profile shows a COVERAGE_STATS_DELTA insight. Which action addresses the cause?
choices: Raise the maximum number of clusters of the warehouse, because missing file statistics are caused by queries that wait in the queue
Add tenant_id to delta.dataSkippingStatsColumns and run ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE DELTA STATISTICS so existing files get statistics
Partition the table by tenant_id, because partition pruning is the only technique that skips files for columns without any statistics
Rewrite the filter with a salting expression, because the insight reports that the filtered column is distributed unevenly across tasks
quiz.explain: COVERAGE_STATS_DELTA means file-skipping statistics are missing or incomplete for the filtered column. Declaring it a statistics column and recomputing statistics lets existing files be skipped. Queue time and skew are different insights.

quiz.q: A 200 GB Delta table is partitioned by an integer hour key, event_hour, with about 9,000 partitions of roughly 20 MB, and scans read thousands of small files. Predictive optimization cannot compact them. The conversion should cause minimal downtime. What should the engineer do?
choices: Run ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY (event_hour), then OPTIMIZE
Add ZORDER BY (event_hour) to a nightly OPTIMIZE, because Z-ordering merges the small files of different partitions into one larger file
Partition the table by event_minute instead, because smaller partitions reduce the number of files that a scan has to open
Run VACUUM with a retention of zero hours, because deleting old versions compacts the small files of every partition
quiz.explain: Predictive optimization cannot compact small files across partitions, so liquid clustering is the route. The conversion minimizes reader and writer downtime, and keeping the keys near the old partition columns avoids a large first reclustering.

days.recap: Start from the performance insight, confirm it in the profile, and fix its cause: key uniqueness, statistics, skew, spill, queue time. Prefer liquid clustering over partitioning and ZORDER, and convert partitioned tables with REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY.

days.title: Least-Privilege ACLs and ABAC Policies with Governed Tags

concepts.heading: Object ACLs: Pick the Lowest Rung That Covers Every Duty
concepts.body: Workspace objects use permission ladders, and least privilege means choosing the lowest rung that covers every required action. For a job the rungs are CAN VIEW (details, settings and results), CAN MANAGE RUN (adds the Spark UI and logs of a run, Run now, Run now with different parameters, and cancel), then CAN MANAGE and IS OWNER (add editing settings, deleting the job and changing permissions). An on-call group that must read logs, rerun with other parameters and cancel but never edit therefore needs CAN MANAGE RUN. A Lakeflow pipeline has CAN VIEW (see it, Spark UI and driver logs), CAN RUN (start and stop updates) and CAN MANAGE; release operators who only start updates need CAN RUN, and developers keep CAN MANAGE. A job has exactly one owner, and a group cannot be the owner, so production jobs are usually owned by a service principal. Remember that CAN MANAGE RUN allows overriding job parameters, so a parameter default is not a security control; restricting the permission is.

concepts.heading: Unity Catalog Privileges: Narrow Grants and What ALL PRIVILEGES Leaves Out
concepts.body: Every access path in Unity Catalog needs USE CATALOG on the catalog and USE SCHEMA on the schema, plus a privilege on the object itself. Grant the narrowest privilege on the narrowest object: a service principal that only refreshes one materialized view needs USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and REFRESH on that view, not SELECT, MODIFY or ownership. Privileges granted on a catalog or schema are inherited by current and future children, so a broad grant is convenient but also reaches objects created later. ALL PRIVILEGES does not include MANAGE, READ METADATA, EXTERNAL USE SCHEMA or EXTERNAL USE LOCATION, which prevents accidental escalation. MANAGE can grant and revoke privileges, transfer ownership and drop the object. READ METADATA is the audit rung: it shows grants, row filters, column masks and ABAC policies without reading data or changing anything. BROWSE only exposes names, comments and tags so people can find an object and request access.

concepts.heading: ABAC: Governed Tags Decide Which Policies Apply
concepts.body: Attribute-based access control moves protection from individual tables to attributes. A governed tag is a key-value pair defined at the account level, and a row filter or column mask policy attached to a catalog, schema or table applies to every table or column in scope whose tags match its condition, such as `MATCH COLUMNS has_tag('pii') AS c`. Databricks recommends attaching policies at the highest applicable level. The TO clause names who is subject to the policy and EXCEPT names who is exempt; exempt principals see unmodified data. Creating a policy needs MANAGE on the securable (or ownership) and EXECUTE on the function. Tags are inherited from the parent catalog or schema, but column tags do not inherit from the table and must be set on the column. Because tagging decides which policies apply, applying a governed tag needs two grants: APPLY TAG on the object and ASSIGN on the tag. Neither lets the steward read data or edit policies.

concepts.heading: Designing ABAC for Cost and for Gaps
concepts.body: A row filter function runs for every row and a column mask for every matched value, so keep functions small. Use SQL functions rather than Python UDFs, simple CASE and boolean logic, and avoid subqueries or joins on large lookup tables, which block broadcast joins. Identity functions such as `is_account_group_member()` are resolved once during query analysis, so model entitlements as groups (for example one group per region) instead of a 90-million-row user-to-store table, and use EXCEPT to skip the function for administrators. The second design question is untagged data. A policy keyed on the pii tag does nothing when the tag is missing, so give new objects a default restrictive tag such as `classification = unverified` through a schema or catalog tag and write a policy that hides everything with that value from all but the stewards. Stewards later change the tag to its real value. Finally, tables with policies must be read by name; path-based access to their files is not supported.

examPoints: A question that lists duties (logs, run with other parameters, cancel, but no edit) is testing the lowest permission rung: CAN MANAGE RUN for jobs, CAN RUN for pipeline updates.
A question where a broad grant fails or a reviewer needs visibility is testing what ALL PRIVILEGES excludes (MANAGE, READ METADATA) and the narrow alternatives REFRESH and READ METADATA.
A question on slow or leaky ABAC is testing small SQL functions with group-based entitlements and EXCEPT, a default restrictive tag for unclassified data, and APPLY TAG plus ASSIGN for stewards.

quiz.q: The group `release_ops` must start and stop updates of the pipeline `orders_pipeline` and open its driver logs, but must not edit its settings or permissions. Which permission on the pipeline follows least privilege?
choices: CAN MANAGE, because stopping a running update is a management action that is not available on the lower permission levels
CAN VIEW, because viewing the driver logs and the Spark UI already includes the right to trigger an update
CAN RUN, which adds starting and stopping updates to viewing the pipeline, its Spark UI and driver logs
IS OWNER, because only the single owner of a pipeline can start an update that someone else created
quiz.explain: CAN RUN covers starting and stopping updates plus the CAN VIEW abilities. Editing settings, deleting and changing permissions begin at CAN MANAGE, and CAN VIEW cannot start updates.

quiz.q: Ingestion teams create tables in the schema `landing` weekly, and stewards classify columns days later. Until then columns with personal data are readable because the ABAC policy matches only the `pii` tag. Which design closes the gap?
choices: Run a weekly audit job that lists the untagged columns and then revokes SELECT from the ingestion group until a steward has reviewed each of them
Set a default tag `classification = unverified` on the schema and add a policy hiding unverified tables from all but the stewards
Grant ASSIGN on the pii tag to the ingestion teams so each of them tags the new columns as part of the table creation
Add the ingestion teams to the EXCEPT clause of the pii policy so that they can control what the new tables expose
quiz.explain: Tables inherit the schema tag, so new objects start restricted and a steward lifts the restriction by setting the real value. An audit finds the gap only afterwards, and exempting or empowering the creators does not protect unclassified data.

days.recap: Least privilege is the lowest rung that covers every duty: CAN MANAGE RUN for jobs, CAN RUN for pipelines, narrow Unity Catalog grants such as REFRESH, and READ METADATA for auditors because ALL PRIVILEGES leaves out MANAGE. ABAC applies row filters and column masks by governed tag; keep policy functions simple with group entitlements and EXCEPT, protect untagged data with a default restrictive tag, and read policy-protected tables by name.

days.title: Anonymization, PII Pipelines, Purging, and Governance (D7): Tags, Comments, Inheritance

concepts.heading: Anonymization versus Pseudonymization
concepts.body: Pseudonymization replaces an identifier with a stand-in but keeps a way back or a way to link records; anonymization removes that possibility. A plain `sha2(phone_number, 256)` is only pseudonymization: a 10-digit number has too few possibilities, so an attacker can hash every candidate and recover the originals. Choose the technique by the analytic need. Suppression (NULL or dropped column) is safe but loses the attribute. Generalization replaces a birth date by an age band or a postal code by its first digits, which still supports distributions and lowers re-identification risk because many people share each value. Hashing with a secret salt or tokenization keeps records linkable. Tokenization stores a random token in the events and the mapping in a tightly governed vault table: authorized support can reverse a token, and an erasure request becomes a small delete in the vault while the large events table stays unchanged. Masks apply at read time, so a copy meant for developers must be materialized with anonymized values; deep and shallow clones are not supported on tables with row filters or column masks.

concepts.heading: A Compliant PII Pipeline
concepts.body: Treat every place where data lands as a potential leak. With Auto Loader in rescue mode, a new field such as `national_id` goes into `_rescued_data` as a JSON blob; a silver step that masks named columns never sees it, so the blob needs its own handling. Lakeflow expectations choose the response to a violating record: warn keeps it and counts it, drop removes it without storing it, fail rolls back the update and stops processing. To block a nine-digit pattern while other records flow and offenders stay available for investigation, tag rows valid or invalid and write the invalid ones to a quarantine table. ABAC masks are evaluated for whoever reads, including a job principal: a pipeline that hashes a masked email gets one constant hash for every row, so exempt the pipeline's service principal with EXCEPT or protect bronze with grants. Stateful operators such as dropDuplicates keep their keys in the checkpoint, outside table protections. Data Classification writes sample values to a system table that only the account admin reads by default.

concepts.heading: Purging: Where Deleted Data Survives
concepts.body: A DELETE is logical. With deletion vectors a small metadata file hides the rows while the Parquet file still holds them, and a VACUUM run right away removes nothing because the current version still references that file. The physical sequence is: DELETE the rows, run `REORG TABLE t APPLY (PURGE)` to rewrite the files so the current version no longer contains the data, then run VACUUM with a retention that covers the purge so older files disappear. Old table versions stay readable until VACUUM passes the retention threshold (default 7 days for data files, 30 days for log history), and a change data feed stores deleted values in `_change_data`, so that history needs cleaning as well. Lowering the check with `retentionDurationCheck.enabled = false` risks breaking long-running readers and concurrent writers, so choose a retention that matches the longest job. Many single-user deletes rewrite the same large files repeatedly; record requests in a control table and delete them in one MERGE. A full refresh of a streaming table cannot serve erasure when the source no longer holds its history.

concepts.heading: D7 Governance: Tags, Comments, and Inheritance
concepts.body: Discoverability comes from metadata. BROWSE, granted on a catalog (typically to all account users), lets people see names, comments and tags of objects and request access, without data access or USE CATALOG. Comments need the owner or MANAGE for catalogs and schemas, but for a view or materialized view only the owner; AI-generated comments exist for tables and columns and need a person to accept them. Tags are stored as plain text and may be replicated globally, so a tag must never hold personal data: put a ticket id there. Securables inherit tags from the catalog or schema, the most specific assignment wins, and column tags do not inherit. Privileges inherit down the hierarchy to current and future children, but metastore-level grants do not inherit to catalogs (READ METADATA is the exception), and ownership does not inherit either. A view's base-table check uses the view owner, so the owner must keep access, and production objects belong to a group or service principal.

examPoints: A question where a hash is called anonymization is testing the brute-force weakness of unsalted hashes, and the choice between generalization, suppression and a tokenization vault by analytic need and erasure.
A question about erased data still found in storage is testing DELETE then REORG TABLE APPLY (PURGE) then VACUUM, plus older versions, change data feed, checkpoints and the 7 and 30 day defaults.
A question on governance is testing BROWSE at catalog level, owner-only comments on views, tags without personal data, inheritance (tags and privileges yes, ownership and column tags no).

quiz.q: A team ran `DELETE FROM customers WHERE id = 42` on a table with deletion vectors enabled and then `VACUUM customers` the same hour. An audit still finds the customer's row in the Parquet files. What closes the gap?
choices: Run `REORG TABLE customers APPLY (PURGE)` to rewrite the files without the row, then run VACUUM past the retention
Run VACUUM again with a retention of zero hours, because the first run skipped files that were deleted a moment before
Run `OPTIMIZE` with a smaller target file size, because only files below the target are rewritten without deleted rows
Disable change data feed on the table, because deletion vectors keep rows only when that feature records the changes
quiz.explain: Deletion vectors mark rows without rewriting the file, so VACUUM finds nothing unreferenced. REORG APPLY (PURGE) rewrites the files, and a later VACUUM removes the old versions once they pass the retention.

quiz.q: An analytics team documents `sha2(phone_number, 256)` as anonymization. A reviewer recovers the numbers by hashing every possible 10-digit value. Which statement is correct?
choices: The hash is irreversible by definition, so the reviewer must have used a copy of the original column
It is only pseudonymized, since a small input space can be enumerated; generalize it or use a token vault
Raising the digest to SHA-512 makes the enumeration of every possible number impossible, so the design only needs a longer hash
The data becomes anonymous once a column mask hides it, since masks rewrite the stored values in the files
quiz.explain: Unsalted hashing of a small input space can be reversed by enumeration, so it stays pseudonymization. Longer digests do not help, and masks apply at read time without changing the stored files.

days.recap: Hashing a small input space is pseudonymization; choose generalization, suppression or a tokenization vault by the analytic need and erasure. Guard PII at every landing place: rescued data, quarantine, masks that hit pipeline principals, checkpoint state. Purge with DELETE, REORG PURGE and VACUUM, and remember versions and change data feed. Governance uses BROWSE, tags without personal data and inheritance rules.

days.title: Diagnosing Slow and Failing Work: Spark UI, Logs, System Tables, Query Profiles

concepts.heading: Reading the Spark UI: Gaps, Skew, Spill
concepts.body: Start with the jobs timeline. A gap of a minute or more in the middle of a pipeline means no Spark job is running while workers are idle but billed. Common causes are non-Spark code, a very complex plan, a malfunctioning cluster or an overloaded driver; the Metrics view tells them apart, because a red driver tile with calm workers marks the driver as the bottleneck. Remedies are a larger driver or less work on it, such as many concurrent streams. For a slow stage, open the longest one and check spill first: spill statistics appear only when the stage spilled, and without them more executor memory is not the fix. Then compare the Max duration with the 75th percentile in Summary Metrics; if Max exceeds it by 50 percent or more, the stage might have skew, with one task running long while other cores sit idle. Adaptive query execution can split skewed partitions in a sort merge join. Executors removed on an autoscaling cluster is normal scale-down unless failures accompany it.

concepts.heading: Logs That Outlive the Cluster
concepts.body: Databricks separates three kinds of compute logging. Compute event logs record lifecycle events such as creation, termination and configuration edits; they are not Spark logs. Driver logs (stdout, stderr and log4j) are what you debug with, and they are viewable while the compute exists. A job cluster terminates after the run, so the on-call engineer finds nothing the next morning unless log delivery to a destination was configured on the cluster before the run. Plan that for production job compute, and remember that secrets are not redacted from driver stdout and stderr, so restrict who can read the logs. The Spark UI has a Streaming tab only while a streaming query is running on that compute; if the tab is missing, the query never started or has stopped, so read the driver logs for the startup exception. A healthy streaming batch is processed within about 80 percent of the trigger interval; processing time near or above the interval builds a backlog.

concepts.heading: Job and Pipeline Evidence in System Tables
concepts.body: System tables answer questions across runs. `system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline` stores the active period of a run in slices of up to one hour, so a long run has several rows with the same run_id, and `result_state` and `termination_code` are filled only in the row that ends the run. Counting repairs therefore filters on a non-NULL result_state and subtracts one per run. A run that never began executing appears with period_start_time equal to period_end_time; its termination_code explains why, for example a concurrency limit or a compute error. `system.compute.node_timeline` holds minute-by-minute utilization per node with a driver flag and memory percentages, so a driver near full memory before an out-of-memory failure points to collect(), toPandas() or a large broadcast. `system.query.history` splits one statement's time into waiting for compute, waiting at capacity, compilation and execution: if only the capacity wait grew, the warehouse queue is the cause, not the SQL.

concepts.heading: Query Profiles and Choosing the Right Tool
concepts.body: Match the symptom to the evidence. For SQL on a warehouse, the query profile shows the operators, time per operator and rows scanned, and is visible to the query owner or to users with at least CAN MONITOR on the warehouse. For a classic cluster stage, use the Spark UI stage page. For many runs over time, use system tables. For a failed task, read the task's output and the driver logs first, then check whether the cause is upstream. A useful order is: find the longest or failed stage, decide between skew, spill, a driver bottleneck and queueing, and only then change settings. Treat the first suspect with care. Executors removed in the timeline can be autoscaling instead of out-of-memory crashes, so check the compute event log first, then the executor and driver logs, before resizing. Increasing memory for a stage without spill, or adding workers for a driver-bound job, costs money without fixing the cause.

examPoints: A question with idle workers and gaps in the jobs timeline is testing the Metrics view for an overloaded driver, not more executors.
A question where one task outlasts 199 others and no spill appears is testing skew (Max above the 75th percentile by 50 percent), with adaptive query execution as the first remedy, not more memory.

A question that needs history across runs is testing system tables: job_run_timeline (end row holds result_state), node_timeline (minute per node), query.history (waiting_at_capacity versus execution).

quiz.q: A stage on a classic cluster runs 14 minutes while 199 of its 200 tasks finish in about 20 seconds. The stage page shows no spill statistics, and Max duration far exceeds the 75th percentile. What is the right conclusion?
choices: Executor memory is too small, so the cluster needs larger worker nodes with more memory available to every core
Autoscaling removed executors during the stage, so the minimum number of workers should be raised for the whole run
The stage shows skew, so let adaptive query execution split the partition or fix the key
The driver is overloaded, so a larger driver node would shorten the idle time between the Spark jobs in the pipeline
quiz.explain: No spill statistics means the stage did not spill, and a Max far above the 75th percentile is the skew signature. Memory or scale changes do not help one oversized task.

quiz.q: A task on a shared SQL warehouse takes twice as long. In `system.query.history` its `execution_duration_ms` is unchanged but `waiting_at_capacity_duration_ms` grew sharply. Which action addresses the cause?
choices: Rewrite the SQL statement with fewer joins, because compilation time dominates the total statement duration here
Run OPTIMIZE on the source tables, because capacity waits are caused by too many small files in the tables
Add warehouse capacity or move the task to a less busy warehouse, because the statement waits in a queue
Increase the task timeout so that the statement keeps its place in the queue without ever being cancelled
quiz.explain: Unchanged execution time with growing capacity wait means the statement queues for warehouse capacity. Query tuning or file layout would not shorten that wait.

days.recap: Diagnose by evidence: jobs timeline gaps plus the Metrics view mean driver, skew shows as Max above the 75th percentile without spill, and spill needs memory or shuffle fixes. Deliver logs before job clusters end. In system tables remember hourly slices and end-row result_state, minute node utilization, and the wait columns of query history.

days.title: Repairs and Parameter Overrides: Fix the Failure Without Redoing the Run

concepts.heading: What a Repair Run Does
concepts.body: A repair re-runs only the unsuccessful tasks and the tasks that depend on them; tasks that succeeded are not repeated, which saves time and compute. Unsuccessful tasks run with the current job and task settings, so fix the notebook path or compute setting first and then repair. If tasks share a job cluster, a repair run creates a new job cluster from the current settings of the original, named with a version suffix such as `my_job_cluster_v1`. Each failed task restarts from the beginning, and Lakeflow Jobs does not make tasks idempotent: a task that appended part of its output before failing can duplicate data, so prefer overwrite or MERGE writes in tasks that may be repaired. A repair is the right tool when the input was correct and a step failed for an external reason, such as a permission problem that is now fixed or a transient outage.

concepts.heading: Parameter Overrides: What They Change and What They Cannot
concepts.body: In the repair dialog you can add or edit parameters for the tasks being repaired; these values override the existing ones for the re-run tasks only, and clearing key and value on a later repair returns a parameter to its original. Successful tasks keep what they computed. An operator who started Run now with `run_date = 2026-10-31` instead of the right day, and whose first two tasks succeeded, cannot fix the data with a repair, because those tasks already consumed the wrong value. Start a new run with correct parameters (and clean up the wrong output). A job parameter default is not a security control: anyone with CAN MANAGE RUN can override it for a manual run, including through the REST API, so restrict permissions instead. From the CLI, `databricks bundle run` takes job parameters with `--params k=v` and runs a slice of tasks with `--only`; a plus suffix adds downstream tasks and a plus prefix adds upstream tasks. That creates a new run and is not a repair.

concepts.heading: Disabled Tasks, Dependencies, and Continuous Jobs
concepts.body: Dependencies are evaluated with the Run if condition of each task. A disabled task is skipped but keeps its configuration; with the default condition, All succeeded, a disabled parent does not satisfy its dependents, so they do not run unless they use a condition such as at least one succeeded. A repair selects tasks by their run state, not by whether they are currently disabled, so a task that completed as skipped in the original run is not picked just because someone re-enabled it. To force it into a repair, list it in `rerun_tasks` of the repair request; otherwise start a new run (or a bundle run with `--only`). A continuous job keeps one run active; after consecutive failures beyond a threshold, Lakeflow Jobs retries with exponential backoff and the Job details pane shows the failure count and the time to the next retry. To resume immediately after the cause is fixed, use Restart run in the UI or pass the job ID in a run-now request in the Jobs API, which starts the job at once and resets the wait.

concepts.heading: Pipelines: Refresh Failed Tables versus Full Refresh
concepts.body: A pipeline update normally processes only new data. When an update fails in one or two tables, use Refresh failed tables, which reruns the tables that failed together with the ones that depend on them, instead of reprocessing everything. A full refresh clears the data of streaming tables, clears their checkpoints and reprocesses all records from the source. It is correct only when the input can recreate the desired state. If a Kafka topic keeps seven days of data while the streaming tables hold two years of history, a full refresh deletes history that cannot be replayed. The same trap exists for erasure requests: deleting at the source and fully refreshing would destroy the historical data. For a transient storage error, refresh the failed tables; for a logic change that must apply to history, check that the source can replay the data, or store the history in a layer the pipeline can reread. Choose the narrowest recovery that restores correctness.

examPoints: A question with a failed middle task and a fixed cause is testing repair: only unsuccessful and dependent tasks rerun, with current settings, and a new version-suffixed job cluster when shared.
A question where an operator typed a wrong parameter and earlier tasks succeeded is testing that a repair override affects only re-run tasks, so a new run is needed.
A question on a failed pipeline table over a source with short retention is testing Refresh failed tables instead of full refresh.

quiz.q: A job `ingest -> transform -> publish` was started with the wrong value `run_date = 2026-10-31`. Ingest and transform succeeded and wrote data for that day, then publish failed on a permission problem that is fixed. The correct date is 2026-11-01. What is the right remedy?
choices: Repair the run and override run_date with the correct value, which re-executes all three tasks
Start a new run with the correct run_date and remove the output written for the wrong day
Repair the run unchanged, because the publish task reads the date again when it executes
Disable the transform task and repair the run, so that every task is evaluated again from scratch
quiz.explain: A repair override changes only the tasks being re-run, and successful tasks are not repeated, so the wrong input already produced wrong data. A new run with the right value fixes it.

quiz.q: A streaming table in a Lakeflow pipeline reads a Kafka topic that keeps seven days of data, and the table holds two years of history. One update failed in a single table because of a transient storage error that is fixed now. What should the team run?
choices: A full refresh of the whole pipeline, so the checkpoints are rebuilt and the failed table is consistent again
A full refresh of only the failed table, since a refresh clears its checkpoint and replays the topic
Refresh failed tables, which reruns the failed table and its dependents without clearing existing data
Delete the streaming table and recreate it from the pipeline source code on the next update
quiz.explain: Refresh failed tables reruns only what failed. A full refresh clears the data and checkpoints and cannot replay two years of history from a seven day topic.

days.recap: Repair reruns failed and dependent tasks with current settings; overrides apply only to re-run tasks, so wrong inputs consumed by successful tasks need a new run. Disabled tasks are not rerun by repair, continuous jobs restart after backoff with Restart run, and pipelines recover with Refresh failed tables, never a full refresh against a source without history.

days.title: Deploying with Bundles and Git Folders CI/CD

concepts.heading: Bundle Deploy Options in CI
concepts.body: A bundle deployment keeps state in the workspace under `~/.bundle/<bundle.name>/<target>`, and its identity is the deployer, bundle name and target; resources are tracked by ID. Renaming `bundle.name` therefore creates a second set of resources next to the old one, with the old schedules still active. Before the first deploy under the new name, bind the existing resources with `databricks bundle deployment bind`, or run bundle destroy for the old deployment.
