The `databricks bundle deploy` options matter in CI: `--fail-on-active-runs` fails if jobs or pipelines in the deployment are running, `--auto-approve` only skips interactive approvals such as deleting resources removed from the configuration, `--force` overrides validations such as the Git branch check (and overwrites a dashboard edited in the workspace), and `--force-lock` breaks a stale deployment lock after a crashed run. Use force-lock only after confirming that no deployment is running. Development mode disables the lock by default; production keeps it. Validate before deploying, and deploy the same commit through each stage.

concepts.heading: Targets, Presets, Permissions and Run Identity
concepts.body: Targets hold per-environment settings. Deployment modes (development, production) set default behaviors, presets customize them (name_prefix, trigger_pause_status, jobs_max_concurrent_runs, tags), and the settings of an individual resource override presets, so a job that declares `pause_status: UNPAUSED` runs on schedule even when the target preset pauses triggers. The order is mode defaults, then presets, then the resource. Permissions can be set in the top-level `permissions` mapping, which Databricks recommends and which uses CAN_VIEW, CAN_MANAGE and CAN_RUN for all supported resources, or inside a resource with its own levels such as CAN_MANAGE_RUN. Permissions cannot overlap: the same user, group or service principal may not appear in both places, so use one place per principal. `run_as` sets the identity of workflows and at the top level or in a target can be a user or service principal, not a group (only a job or pipeline's own run_as accepts a group); production should use a service principal so that the right to run workflows is separate from the person who deployed. If the deployer is not the run_as identity, some resource types are restricted.

concepts.heading: Git Folders: What They Do and How They Stay Current
concepts.body: A Git folder synchronizes files at a branch: notebooks, modules and configuration. It does not define jobs, pipelines, compute or permissions. For code only, a production Git folder is enough; for whole workflows, per-environment settings and promotion of one commit, Databricks recommends bundles, and the two combine. A production Git folder is created by an admin for a repository and branch, run under a service principal with its own Git credential, and shared with run permission for users. A Git folder does not update itself: after a pull request merges into the deployment branch, an external CI service such as GitHub Actions calls the Repos API to update the folder. Without an external service, a scheduled job running a small notebook with the Databricks SDK updates it, which is simple but can lag by up to the schedule interval. Personal credentials and personal folders disappear with the person, so automation must not depend on them.

concepts.heading: Resolving Git Conflicts Safely
concepts.body: When a pull conflicts with local edits in a Git folder, resolve merge conflicts in the UI: choose the lines to keep, mark the file resolved and continue, or abort and try again. Nothing is lost that you did not choose to drop. Reset is a different operation: it is equivalent to `git reset --hard` combined with `git push --force`, so the selected branch takes the contents and history of another branch and the remote branch is reset too. If two engineers work on the same remote branch, a reset by one silently removes the other's commits from the shared history. Rebase also ends with a force push, which is why Databricks recommends merge for people new to Git because it does not rewrite history. In a CI/CD design, developers work in user-level Git folders on their own branches, merge through pull requests, and only the automation touches the production folder, so conflicts and force pushes never reach production.

examPoints: A question with two stale or duplicate deployments is testing bundle identity (name, target, deployer): rename creates new resources, stale locks need --force-lock, and --fail-on-active-runs protects running work.
A question about conflicting settings is testing precedence (mode, then presets, then the resource), one place for permissions, and a service principal for run_as.
A question on production folders is testing service principal credentials, Repos API or scheduled-job updates, merge versus reset, and Git folder for code versus bundle for resources.

quiz.q: A release pipeline deploys a bundle to `prod`, and scheduled jobs from the previous release may still be running. The team does not want the deployment to update jobs and pipelines while runs are in flight. Which option expresses this?
choices: `--auto-approve`, which makes the deployment wait until active runs have completed before it continues
`--force-lock`, which stops active runs so that the deployment lock can be acquired without a conflict
`--force`, which reschedules the active runs so that they continue with the updated definitions
`--fail-on-active-runs`, which fails the deployment when jobs or pipelines in it are running
quiz.explain: The flag fails the deployment if deployed jobs or pipelines are running. Auto-approve only skips prompts, force overrides validations, and force-lock breaks a stale lock.

quiz.q: A platform team wants a production Git folder to follow its deployment branch after each merged pull request, with no person's identity involved. An external CI service can reach the workspace. Which design fits?
choices: A personal Git folder of the release engineer, pulled manually after every merge to keep an audit trail
A production Git folder run by a service principal, updated by CI through the Repos API after merges
A reset of the production Git folder from the UI after each merge, which keeps its history in line
A bundle deployed from the engineer's laptop, because bundles are the only way to update a Git folder
quiz.explain: A service principal with its own Git credential owns the production folder, and CI calls the Repos API after the merge. Personal folders and manual resets depend on a person, and a reset rewrites history.

days.recap: Bundle identity is deployer, name and target; renames duplicate resources, stale locks need force-lock, and fail-on-active-runs guards in-flight work. Resource settings beat presets, which beat mode defaults, with permissions declared once and run_as a service principal. Git folders sync code under a service principal via Repos API or a scheduled job; use merge, not reset, and bundles for resources.

days.title: Table Layout and Dimensional Models: Delta, Iceberg, Materialized Views, Metric Views

concepts.heading: Choosing a Layout and Fighting Small Files
concepts.body: Layout follows data size and query pattern. Databricks says not to partition tables under 1 TB, and between 1 and 100 TB prefers liquid clustering; each partition should hold at least 1 GB, and partitioning suits low or known cardinality columns such as dates. A multi-tenant table of 600 GB with 5,000 uneven tenants averages about 120 MB per tenant, so partitioning by tenant creates files that compaction cannot merge across partition boundaries; cluster on tenant_id instead. Small files from frequent streaming commits are handled by optimized writes (a shuffle before the write, at some latency cost), auto compaction (runs synchronously on the writing cluster after a write), scheduled OPTIMIZE, and predictive optimization for Unity Catalog managed tables, which runs asynchronously on serverless compute. These are table properties, so they apply to every writer. For an append-only job with strict latency, turn auto compaction off in the job session and let predictive optimization work in the background; MERGE, UPDATE and DELETE always keep auto compaction and optimized writes on.

concepts.heading: File Size and Managed Iceberg
concepts.body: For tables without a configured target, Databricks tunes the target file size by table size: 256 MB below 2.56 TB, growing linearly to 1 GB at 10 TB, and 1 GB above. When the target grows, OPTIMIZE does not rewrite existing files just because the target moved, so a growing table can hold older, smaller files; this is expected. Setting `delta.targetFileSize` (for Iceberg `iceberg.targetFileSize`) fixes the target but switches autotuning off for that table. It is a best-effort target: for managed tables on a SQL warehouse or a recent runtime, only OPTIMIZE respects it, so an ordinary INSERT can still write other sizes. Iceberg tables created in Unity Catalog are managed Iceberg tables, writable from Databricks and from external engines through the Iceberg REST catalog. Unity Catalog manages snapshot expiration and compaction, predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE, and liquid clustering is the layout feature, with `PARTITION BY` columns interpreted as clustering keys. The layout is decided once in Unity Catalog, not per engine.

concepts.heading: Dimensional Modeling in the Lakehouse
concepts.body: For a new lakehouse Databricks recommends against heavily normalized third normal form models in favor of star or snowflake schemas: a fact table with one row per event at a declared grain, numeric measures and keys, and denormalized dimension tables used to filter and group. Primary key, foreign key and unique constraints are informational; only NOT NULL and CHECK are enforced. A fact row that arrives before its customer is accepted, so referential integrity is the pipeline's job: insert an inferred placeholder member, map to an Unknown member, or quarantine. An SCD Type 2 dimension (`__START_AT`, `__END_AT`, where `__END_AT` is NULL for the current version) has several rows per customer, and joining a fact on the business key alone repeats each order once per version and inflates revenue. Use a point-in-time join within the validity range, filter to the current version, or store the version's surrogate key in the fact at load time.

concepts.heading: Materialized Views and Metric Views
concepts.body: A materialized view stores a query result and refreshes it incrementally where the query and sources allow, otherwise by full recompute, so dashboards avoid scanning a 4-billion-row fact table. The stored grain decides which questions it can answer. SUM and COUNT are additive and roll up; averages, ratios and distinct counts are not, because the average of group averages is not the overall average. Store the components (sum and count) at the finest needed grain, and compute the ratio after the roll-up. One view at the finest grain serves several dashboards with a single refresh to maintain. Unity Catalog metric views are a semantic layer: a measure such as revenue divided by distinct customers is defined once, separate from the dimensions, and users group by any available field at query time while the engine builds the right computation. A standard view locks in its grouping, so each team that regroups it gets numbers that cannot be compared.

examPoints: A question on many small files from a stream is testing optimized writes, auto compaction and predictive optimization on managed tables, not a manual repartition or more partitions.
A question on partitioning a table of a few hundred GB is testing the under 1 TB and 1 GB per partition guidance, with liquid clustering on the filter column.
A question on inflated revenue is testing SCD Type 2 versions in a join; a question on cross-team metric differences is testing metric views and additive components in materialized views.

quiz.q: A fact table holds 600 GB of events from 5,000 uneven tenants, about 120 MB per tenant on average, and most queries filter on one tenant_id. A designer proposes `PARTITIONED BY (tenant_id)`. What should the team do instead?
choices: Partition by tenant_id and run OPTIMIZE daily, since compaction merges the small files across partition boundaries
Partition by the event timestamp as well, so that each tenant directory is divided into smaller parts
Use liquid clustering on tenant_id, because a table under 1 TB with tiny partitions should not be partitioned
Keep a separate table per tenant, which gives every customer files of at least the target file size
quiz.explain: Partitions should hold at least 1 GB and under 1 TB tables should not be partitioned. Files cannot be combined across partitions, so clustering on tenant_id gives data skipping without tiny directories.

quiz.q: A report joins `fact_orders` to an SCD Type 2 table `dim_customer` with `ON f.customer_id = d.customer_id`, and revenue by segment is too high. Declaring customer_id as the primary key of the dimension did not help. What is the cause and fix?
choices: The join matches every version and keys are informational; use the valid version or a surrogate key
The primary key was declared after loading, so the table must be recreated for the optimizer to deduplicate the matches
The fact table has duplicate order rows, so a DISTINCT on the order id before the join removes the extra revenue
The report must use a broadcast hint, because a shuffle join produces more output rows than a broadcast join
quiz.explain: A Type 2 dimension keeps several rows per customer, and a primary key is informational so it neither rejects them nor changes the join. Join within the validity range, to the current version, or on a surrogate key.

days.recap: Do not partition under 1 TB; cluster on the filter column and fight small files with optimized writes, auto compaction and predictive optimization. File size is autotuned unless fixed, and managed Iceberg shares the layout in Unity Catalog. Model facts and dimensions as stars, treat constraints as informational, join SCD2 by validity, store additive components in materialized views, and define measures once in metric views.

days.title: Final Review: Decision Cheat-Sheet Across the Nine Domains

concepts.heading: D1-D3: Build, Ingest, Transform (47%)
concepts.body: Code and pipelines. Bundles package modular Python with pinned dependencies. Pick a Pandas UDF for vectorized work, a SQL or Unity Catalog function for reuse and governance. Streaming table for append-only incremental input, materialized view for results recomputed or incrementally maintained from changing sources; AUTO CDC gives SCD 1 or 2 with ordering by a sequence column. Stateful streaming needs a watermark to bound state, the output mode that fits the aggregation, a checkpoint per query, and idempotent foreachBatch writes. Ingestion: Auto Loader for files, Lakeflow Connect for databases and SaaS, Lakehouse Federation to query without moving data, OpenSharing and Clean Rooms to share without copies. Transformation: VARIANT for semi-structured payloads, ai_query for model calls in pipelines, expectations (warn, drop, fail) plus quarantine for quality. Jobs: If/Else and For Each for control flow, job clusters or serverless for compute, repair for failed tasks.

concepts.heading: D4-D5: Monitor and Optimize (25%)
concepts.body: Monitoring uses system tables (billing, audit, query history, node_timeline, job_run_timeline), the pipeline event log, the REST API, CLI and SDK, and the Jobs UI and API; use alerts on query results for thresholds. Remember hourly slices and that result_state is set on the end row. Optimization starts with ownership of the work: managed tables with predictive optimization automate OPTIMIZE and VACUUM, and liquid clustering replaces partitioning and ZORDER for new tables under most patterns (cluster on the filter columns, CLUSTER BY AUTO when the pattern changes). Do not partition below 1 TB. Cache repeated reads, but the cache does not replace layout. Change Data Feed gives row-level changes for downstream consumers and costs storage. Read the query profile or Spark UI before tuning: skew (Max above the 75th percentile by 50 percent), spill, driver bottleneck, queue wait. Choose the cheapest fix that matches the evidence.

concepts.heading: D6-D7: Secure and Govern (13%)
concepts.body: Pick the lowest permission rung: CAN MANAGE RUN for job operators, CAN RUN for pipeline operators, REFRESH on a single materialized view, READ METADATA for auditors. ALL PRIVILEGES excludes MANAGE. ABAC combines governed tags with row filter and column mask policies at the highest sensible level, with TO and EXCEPT, small SQL functions and group entitlements; add a default restrictive tag for unclassified data and read policy-protected tables by name. Applying a governed tag needs APPLY TAG and ASSIGN. A hash of a small input space is only pseudonymization; generalize, suppress or tokenize. Erase with DELETE, REORG PURGE and VACUUM, and mind history, change data feed and checkpoint state. Governance: BROWSE on the catalog for discovery, no personal data in tags, comments on views by the owner only, inheritance flows down for privileges and tags but not for ownership or column tags.

concepts.heading: D8-D9: Debug, Deploy, Model (15%)
concepts.body: Debug by evidence: jobs timeline gaps with a red driver mean the driver is the bottleneck, skew and spill are on the stage page, node_timeline shows memory before a failure, query history separates queue wait from execution. Repair reruns failed and dependent tasks with current settings; overrides do not change what earlier tasks consumed; pipelines use Refresh failed tables unless the source can replay history. Bundles carry resources and targets: mode, then presets, then the resource wins; run_as a service principal; fail-on-active-runs for in-flight work and force-lock only for a stale lock; a rename duplicates resources. Git folders sync code: production folders use a service principal, CI or a scheduled job updates them, and merge beats reset. Model as a star schema, treat keys as informational, join SCD2 by validity range, keep additive components in materialized views, and define shared measures once in metric views.

examPoints: Before answering, name the domain: then ask what the evidence is (Spark UI, system tables, event log), what the lowest sufficient privilege or narrowest recovery is, and what the table layout and size imply.

Traps recur: full refresh without source history, ALL PRIVILEGES assumed to include MANAGE, an informational constraint assumed to be enforced, a repair assumed to fix an earlier wrong input, partitioning small tables.

Features marked Beta or Public Preview are not the keyed answer: use the generally available mechanism (catalog, schema or table-level ABAC policies, managed tables, bundles) unless the question states otherwise.

quiz.q: A streaming table reads a Kafka topic with seven days of retention and holds two years of history. A privacy request names one subject. An engineer plans to delete the subject at the source and run a full refresh of the table. What is the problem?
choices: A full refresh replays only the seven days left in the topic, so the older history is lost
A full refresh keeps all existing rows and appends the topic again, so the subject remains in all of the older rows
Deleting at the source is not allowed for a Kafka topic, so the request must be handled in the bronze layer only, never later
The refresh succeeds but leaves the subject in the checkpoints, so VACUUM must be run on the streaming table instead of it
quiz.explain: A full refresh clears data and checkpoints and reprocesses what the source still holds. With seven days of retention that destroys two years of history; erasure should be a targeted delete plus purge.

quiz.q: A team lead holds ALL PRIVILEGES on the catalog `prod` and owns nothing in it. The lead runs `GRANT SELECT ON TABLE prod.sales.orders TO analysts` and gets a permission error. What explains this and what is the least-privilege fix?
choices: Grants on tables require metastore admin rights, so a metastore admin must run every grant in the catalog
ALL PRIVILEGES covers only reads and writes of data, so granting it again on the table repeats the error
ALL PRIVILEGES excludes MANAGE, which is what permits granting; give MANAGE on the catalog or the schema
The lead needs ownership of the table, since MANAGE on a parent container is not inherited by the children
quiz.explain: ALL PRIVILEGES excludes MANAGE, READ METADATA and the external use privileges. Granting needs ownership or MANAGE, which also applies to current and future children when granted on a container.

days.recap: Final check: name the domain, read the evidence before changing settings, choose the lowest sufficient privilege and the narrowest recovery, size the layout from the data volume, and prefer generally available mechanisms. Watch the repeated traps: full refresh without history, ALL PRIVILEGES without MANAGE, informational constraints, repairs of earlier wrong inputs, early partitioning.
